#2712. Giants earn their most impressive win of the season with upset of Jaguars

The NFC East-leading Giants made a statement today against the Jaguars.

In a game that few expected the Giants to win, New York took a 10-3 first quarter lead and never relinquished it, turning in an impressive performance and beating the Jaguars 23-18.

The Giants were aided by two highly controversial touchdown calls: Giants quarterback Jameis Winston got a fourth-and-goal tush push touchdown despite his helmet appearing to be down before the ball crossed the goal line, and Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington was denied a touchdown catch despite appearing to have possession with his feet down in bounds.

But the two controversies shouldn’t overshadow that this Giants team is far better than anyone expected. They’re 6-3-1 and in total control of the NFC East, and today they earned their most impressive win yet.

The Jaguars fall to 7-3, and despite the loss they’re still the overwhelming favorites to win the AFC South. This loss will hurt in the AFC playoff seeding, however, as they’re now long shots to earn the No. 1 seed.

Both the Giants and the Jaguars look like playoff teams. This was a hard-fought game between two opponents that expect to still be playing well into January. And maybe February.

#2707. Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off

As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.

On platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.

Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.

On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.

The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.

The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.

"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.

The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.

In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

Amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. #2698. Thunder are NBA's deepest team, but not even they can weather all these injuries

MIAMI — It became immediately evident as soon as the layup lines started.

On one side, the Miami Heat were mostly at full strength, the lone exception being their new star and Most Valuable Player candidate Giannis Antetokounmpo missing his first game of the season.

On the other: the Oklahoma City Thunder, who dressed only nine players.

Of the five players who opened the season as starters, four — Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren and Cason Wallace — missed the game.

It was no surprise, therefore, that the Thunder could not keep up with Miami, which blitzed past Oklahoma City with relative ease Sunday, Nov. 22, 123-113.

It was never close. This was the Thunder's sixth loss in their last eight games, in what has become their least productive stretch in more than three seasons — basically since they became legitimate and ubiquitous championship contenders.

Entering the 2026-27 season, the Thunder were the deepest team in the NBA. But as Oklahoma City keeps sliding down the standings – the loss dropped the Thunder to 10-7 and ninth in the Western Conference, their lowest position since Nov. 4, 2023 – it's becoming clear that even they cannot withstand this many injuries.

The latest player to go down was the one Oklahoma City can least afford to miss. Gilgeous-Alexander, the reigning two-time consecutive Most Valuable Player, suffered a back contusion two days earlier in a win over the Pelicans.

The good news is that Gilgeous-Alexander did participate in his pregame shootaround, in which he put up dozens of shots from different spots on the floor. He didn't appear to have any long-term lingering effects, and all indications are he won't miss extended time.

The bad news is that there really is no way to replace his impact.

"I think the first thing is having a set of principles that transcend circumstances," Thunder coach Mark Daigneault said Sunday when asked how his team will need to weather this stretch. "I think  that's important when you're in unpredictable circumstances. That's what makes you feel at home and makes you feel comfortable. It makes you feel secure; it makes you feel confident – is when you have a way of operating, a way of playing, a way of thinking."

While Daigneault is right, an established identity does go a long way, at some point, identity and culture will never be able to make up for a deficiency in talent. And with this many injuries to both stars and key contributors, this is precisely the disadvantage with which the Thunder are operating.

Against Miami, the Thunder did have six different players reach double figures in scoring. What they lacked, however, was someone who could control the game and get to his spots (like Gilgeous-Alexander so smoothly does), or a player who created opportunities for his teammates. The Thunder did not have a player to surpass 5 assists in the game.

Heat center Bam Adebayo, by comparison, dished out 12 on his way to a 24-point, 15-rebound triple-double.

And, yes, it is November, so players will presumably get healthy. There's plenty of time to claw back up the standings. But in order for that to happen, the team simply will need its abysmal injury luck to reverse. Because it's not just about getting players back, they'll need to work their way back into game shape and they'll need to rediscover their chemistry on the floor.

Oklahoma City was so depleted that by the time the game was out of reach late in the fourth, Daigneault opted to empty his bench with more than six minutes to play. But since there were only four reserves available, forward Micah Peavy, who started the game, had to stay on the floor.

"It's also an acceptance of what the circumstance are," Daigneault said. "And we have to reframe the challenge to what the circumstances are: you've got to be a team that can play the hand that you're dealt. And this is the hand we were dealt. I think not asking for sympathy, not making excuses and just figuring out the best way to operate gives us the best chance to continue to be competitive."

That's all fine and good. But these Thunder won't compete in the West against the Spurs or the Lakers unless they get healthy.

#2696. Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns

Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta said. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

Mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the company to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

"Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

Mehta ranks No. 876 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 8.1%. See Devon Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. ET's cash distribution for Q3 2026 was 34.25 cents per common unit, up more than 3% year-over-year. At an annualized distribution of $1.37 per share, Energy Transfer yields more than 7%.

TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer with a price target of $25. The company delivered better-than-expected Q3 results and announced the 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) South Mississippi Pipeline, a 215-mile, 36-inch natural gas line linking the Perryville Hub to the Florida Gas Transmission (FGT) network, Gabelman said. The project is supported by 20-year firm transportation agreements and is expected to enter service in 2030. ET expects to ultimately own 51% of the $1.6 billion project.

#2695. Broncos move to 8-2 with 38-24 victory over Raiders

The Raiders gave the Broncos plenty to handle on Sunday, but in the end, Denver’s defense came through to put the game away.

A pick-six off of Fernando Mendoza late in the fourth quarter sealed the Broncos’ 38-24 victory.

The Raiders got down 17-0 early but came back to tie the game up at 17-17 midway through the third quarter. The Broncos responded by ripping off a pair of touchdowns, one of which came off a turnover on downs in Denver territory when Mendoza’s pass on fourth-and-2 fell incomplete.

But Las Vegas wasn’t done, scoring on a 7-yard pass from Mendoza with 4:29 left in the contest. Then the defense got a stop, setting up a potential game-tying drive just before the two-minute warning.

However, after that short break, Mendoza was looking for Tre Tucker when his pass was instead picked off by Ja’Quan McMillan — who returned it for a game-sealing, 35-yard pick-six.

Broncos quarterback Bo Nix finished the contest 19-of-35 for 225 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Evan Engram led with 74 yards on six catches. Running back Jonah Coleman had 111 yards on 24 carries plus four catches for 18 yards.

On the other side, Mendoza finished 18-of-37 for 267 yards with three touchdowns and one pick in his second start. He was sacked five times. His first touchdown pass went to Ashton Jeanty, who had 90 yards on five catches to go along with 79 yards on 11 carries. His 46-yard run was his longest of the season.

Jack Bech caught eight passes for 88 yards.

With the win, the Broncos move to 8-2. They’ll have a short week, as they’ll face the Steelers on the road for next week’s Black Friday game.

The Raiders fall to 4-7. They’ll be on the road again next week in primetime, with the matchup against the Browns flexed to Sunday Night Football.

#2684. Lakers get encouraging Austin Reaves update as star nears return

LOS ANGELES – Austin Reaves has been ruled out for a fifth straight game ahead of Monday's contest against the Utah Jazz, but there was an encouraging sight in El Segundo on Sunday afternoon.

Reaves stood at midcourt on the Los Angeles Lakers' practice floor at UCLA Health Training Center, took off his gold practice jersey and conversed with assistant coach Greg St. Jean as he walked over to the left corner. From there, the 6-foot-5 shooting guard was running drills, coming off screens and working with two-way center Carson Cooper.

"We didn't do anything live, but he was a full participant," head coach JJ Redick said.

Redick went on to say that Reaves' practice day consisted mostly of "cleaning up some stuff" followed by two sets of defensive and offensive breakdowns before finishing the day by getting shots up.

The Lakers star has been sidelined since landing awkwardly on his left heel midway through the third quarter of their road win against the Milwaukee Bucks on Wednesday, Nov. 11. X-rays came back negative that night and both Reaves and team medical staff opted against further imaging.

He's been considered day-to-day with a left heel bone bruise and contusion since, though Redick said Sunday that Reaves has been making progress in his recovery.

"They're doing a great job of figuring out the most comfortable insert and the most comfortable shoe," he said. "Finding that right combination."

Redick's insight is particularly valuable in this instance, considering he went through a similar injury himself when he suffered a bone bruise on the bottom of his heel in the last game of the regular season while playing with the Los Angeles Clippers.

"I had to play with it in the playoffs and was taking Toradol shots before the game. It was super painful," he said. "His is in a different spot, it's on the medial side so it's not on the bottom of the foot, but it's really just a comfort/pain issue."

The Lakers can't get Reaves back in the lineup soon enough. Quentin Grimes has had an impressive stretch stepping up in the Wichita State and Oklahoma product's absence, most notably a career-high 47-point game on 10 made 3s while leading the Lakers to an overtime comeback win over the Charlotte Hornets, their overall offense has suffered.

Luka Dončić, the early frontrunner for MVP, has struggled in particular the last two games and has looked downright fatigued at times to keep up his torrid start to the season. He's turned the ball over 20 times in the last three games. And collectively, the Lakers have shot the ball poorly. Dončić, Sandro Mamukelashvili and Jake LaRavia have all seen their 3-point percentages plummet over the last week after looking automatic from deep not long before then.

The stat that stands out the most to Redick: For the first 12 games, the Lakers had the top-rated halfcourt offense in the league. Reaves was on the floor for 70% of those possessions. Over the last seven, their halfcourt offense has dipped to fourth at 120.5 points per possession; Reaves has been on the floor for 9% of that time.

"Who would've thought that not having an elite offensive player, All-Star level player, would hurt your offense?" Redick prosed sarcastically. "That's crazy to me. We're gonna be fine."

The Lakers have been able to continue winning without Reaves, but now it looks like he's getting closer to his return, potentially at some point in their four-game road trip. That would be perfect timing as the Lakers are set to take on the San Antonio Spurs, Memphis Grizzlies and Houston Rockets in that span – all of which are currently top teams in the Western Conference.

Reaves has made the most of his new role as the unquestioned No. 2 in LA this season. In his 12 games played this season, he's averaged 24.7 points on 51.3% shooting (40.9% from deep) to go along with 3.3 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 1.2 steals per game. The Lakers have struggled to replace that production in the four games he's missed, even with Grimes' hot streak.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Lakers get encouraging Austin Reaves update as star nears return

#2678. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2674. Giants on right side of controversial call that denied Jaguars touchdown

Four of the most-dreaded words in the NFL — is it a touchdown? — helped decide the Giants-Jaguars game.

A third-down pass to Jaguars star Parker Washington early in the fourth quarter was ruled incomplete even though Washington dragged both feet in the end zone before his elbow landed out of bounds. But the officials ruled the ball was loose on the field and the replay booth did not overturn it, determining that Washington did not complete the process of the catch.

"The game's over? That might have been a catch," Giants safety Jevon Holland admitted after a 23-18 win. "That was a hell of a play. When they called it out, I was like, 'Alright.' Shoutout Vegas, man. I don't know."

New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips (22) defends Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) during a game on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Brooklyn. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips (22) defends Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in Brooklyn, N.Y. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

"He was out — clear as day — and he bobbled the ball too," Phillips said.

CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore, a former referee, thought it should have been called a touchdown.

"I see the ball move a little bit," Steratore said on the TV broadcast, "but I did not think that he lost possession of the football. I have right foot down, tap with the left foot, yes the ball moves a little but the right hand, in my opinion, continues to keep that secure enough. I think it's a touchdown."

"I felt good about it, but it didn't go our way," Washington said. "You can't hang your head on that."

Jaguars head coach Liam Coen said he was "told that the ball switched hands, so that was what it came down to."

#2673. Lakers vs. Jazz Preview: Seeking vengeance

The Lakers (14-3) will play the Utah Jazz (3-14) once again on Tuesday. This will be the final matchup between the two Western Conference teams, with the series tied 1-1.

The Lakers have a much friendlier schedule this week than they've had over the last two. They had two days off — which feels like a rarity this season — leading up to the Jazz game and will get a three-day break before facing the San Antonio Spurs in an NBA Cup matchup on Friday.

Needless to say, it's well deserved for Luka Dončić and the team, who have been grinding hard to stack up wins over the last few weeks. The one game that really got away from them was the most recent loss to the Jazz. L.A. has the opportunity to get Utah back and here are the x-factors to look out for:

AR has been badly missed in these last few games and it has caught up on the Lakers. His absence has put more pressure on Dončić to carry the offense which the superstar has done a stellar job in. Fortunately, Luka has gotten help from Quentin Grimes who has stepped up big time.

With Reaves expected to return in the next two games, the Lakers' offense balances out and that would be more trouble for the Jazz, who benefited from Luka having his worst offensive performance in their last meeting. Hopefully the Lakers get a much-needed boost with the return of their second-best player. They could use his scoring and playmaking against a Jazz team that didn't have an answer for him last time.

The center is averaging just 6.0 points in 29.6 minutes against the Jazz this season — which is a far cry from his usual 14.3 per game. It's as if Jazz head coach Will Hardy knows exactly how to contain him and that's something the Lakers and Kessler need to figure out ahead of Monday's game.

It would be nice to see Walker break out of his slump against the Jazz since that'll remove the pressure off Dončić and possibly Reaves. Remember, they still have the 20th-best defensive rating in the league and have no business keeping up with the purple and gold offensively. They also haven't had Lauri Markkanen and some of their other front court pieces, so it would be ideal if the Lakers can take advantage of that.

Not to take credit away from the Jazz but fatigue played a huge factor in the Lakers' recent loss to them. Yes, both teams were on the second night of a back-to-back, but it felt like the purple and gold were a step slower and it made sense because they played in overtime the night before. Hopefully, that won't be the case against the Jazz on Monday.

Having already played each other twice in a month, these two squads are quite familiar with each other now. The Lakers can't allow Keyonte George to drop more than 30 points on them again and have someone like Svi Mykhailiuk have his way. They'll be fighting hard for this one, hoping to get contributions from everyone on the team.

Let's see if the Lakers can indeed exact revenge against the Jazz on Monday.

Reaves will be out for the Lakers yet again with a heel bruise. He's the only player on the injury report.

As for the Jazz, Jaren Jackson Jr. (MCL tear), Lauri Markkanen (hand fracture) and Jusuf Nurkic (plantar plate tear) are all out.

#2670. Aaron Rodgers calls DK Metcalf's ejection "disappointing," won't comment on message to him

On certain subjects, Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers doesn’t stop talking. On other topics, he won’t say a single word.

Regarding Sunday’s ejection of Steelers receiver DK Metcalf from the 19-16 loss to the Eagles, Rodgers said far close to nothing than something.

“That was disappointing,” Rodgers told reporters. “Obviously, we love DK. And I don’t know what was going on out there, what was happening. But, yeah, we can’t have two of those.”

“I’m not going to tell you that,” Rodgers said. “I’m going to talk to DK. We’re real good friends, so.”

The “I’m not going to tell you that” was unnecessary, but on brand. Rodgers flashes that aspect of his personality from time to time. And it surely will make those who have to ask him questions on a regular basis not miss him after he retires following the current season.

Besides, why is it such a secret? Rodgers already said it was “disappointing” and that “we can’t have” that. He could have just said that’s the message.

Really, what else would the message be? Metcalf needs to control his emotions. Given that Rodgers has been willing to call out others when it’s required, why should Metcalf be exempt?

Maybe that’s exactly what Metcalf needs in order to keep him from doing it again.

#2666. Mavericks vs Jazz Recap: 3 things to know from the Mavericks 116-114 win against the Jazz

The Dallas Mavericks survived Sunday night, defeating the Utah Jazz 116-114 in Salt Lake City. Dallas has now won three in a row after getting blown out in three straight, stabilizing themselves a bit after things looked rocky after the Mavericks were destroyed by the Celtics last week.

The Mavericks didn't get off to a great start and they certainly didn't have a great finish, but at least the middle parts were fun! Cooper Flagg led Dallas with 28 points in what ended up being a well-rounded effort.

Dallas controlled the middle parts of the game with a swarming defense that got the team out in transition. Utah has a lot of talented guards, but no steady hand to lead the offense. Combine that with the Mavericks penchant for playing the passing lanes aggressively, and the Mavericks were able to turn defense into offense quickly.

It also led to a balanced scoring attack despite Flagg's showing. Dallas had five players in double-figures, all of the starters, and 32 assists on 43 made field goals.

Unfortunately most of the talk about this one will be about the final two minutes, where the Mavericks almost blew what seemed like an insurmountable 16-point lead. Santi Aldama finished a fastbreak layup with about two minutes left in the game to put Dallas up 114-98, and the Jazz's second unit, specifically Svi Mykhailiuk, went ballistic. Backup guard Isaiah Collier made a three, then Mykhailiuk scored nine straight points, making three free throws after getting fouled on a three, then back-to-back three pointers.

Dallas kept throwing the ball away, and coach Dusty May didn't call a timeout to put his starters back in until a Mykhailiuk three made it 114-109 with under 40 seconds left. Another bad turnover gave Utah the ball down two and Collier went full-court against Caleb Martin and scored to tie the game. Ace Bailey committed a bone-headed foul on the next Mavericks possession, allowing Flagg to make the game-winning free throws with 3.6 seconds left. A contested three pointer from Kyle Filipowski hit the back-iron of the rim and the Mavericks escaped with a win.

There's a lot to talk about with this one, but here's the three to know.

Dusty May has undoubtedly done a great job with the Mavericks. A team that looked dead in the water last season with an aimless roster past Flagg has been reset with a new foundation and leadership. The Mavericks are 10-7, competing for a playoff spot early in the season. That is absolutely a success for first-year coach May.

Unfortunately the fourth quarter was not his finest moment. May had several opportunities during Utah's comeback to call a timeout and maybe get some starters back in the game. After Mykhailiuk made three free throws to get the game in single digits with 1:08 left, Dallas could have subbed at least Flagg back in or called a timeout after the last Mykhailiuk free throw. Then when Mykhailiuk made another three with 37.4 left and the score 114-109, May let his backup unit continue and Walter Clayton Jr. committed a brutal turnover, and the Jazz called a timeout and then May put his starters back in.

It was a bit bizarre to watch in real time, especially since the Mavericks had timeouts to spare. It was a good reminder that May is new to this too, at least at the professional level. He is not infallible and rookie mistakes are just part of it, coaches too not just players. It was admirable of May to try and steal some rest for his guys on the second night of a back-to-back in high altitude in Salt Lake City, but it didn't work out. The Jazz bailed the Mavericks out, so in the end no harm, no foul. But those final two minutes were brutal.

Dallas has a lot of athletes on the team, and even if the fundamentals of the Mavericks defense don't always hold game-to-game or even possession-to-possession, it's clear May and the coaching staff want this Mavericks team to exploit their athletic gifts.

The Mavericks play the passing lanes very aggressively. Sometimes the gambles cost them, see some of the tape from the Mavericks recent three game losing streak. But against an overwhelmed and overmatched Jazz team, it can look great. Dallas had 16 steals on the night, which led to 19 fastbreak points. Flagg did a lot of damage in transition, as did Zaccharie Risacher, who had 15 points and multiple dunks.

Every starter for Dallas tonight scored in double-figures — Flagg led the way with 28, Caleb Martin had 13, Daniel Gafford had 10, Risacher had 15 and Kyrie Irving had 16. Dallas didn't get much from the bench, but the starting unit played really well together, and their unselfish play was really fun to watch, as the ball was really moving.

Not only did every starter have at least 10 points, but every starter had at least two assists! Martin, Gafford, and Flagg each had four assists and Irving had eight. It really helps that Flagg and Irving are tremendous off-ball players that are not only willing off-ball players, but enthusiastic off-ball players — they do the work when they don't have the ball to help their teammates get open looks or create opportunities for themselves or others.

#2665. 49ers star turned the NFL’s stingiest defense into his MVP highlight reel

MEXICO CITY – The 49ers came to Mexico to deliver a message that will be heard across the NFL. Anybody planning on representing the NFC in the Super Bowl had better be ready to win in Santa Clara.

On Sunday night, the Vikings got a look at what that might take. Brock Purdy threw three touchdown passes against the league's stingiest defense, and the 49ers rolled to a 35-10 win that put them in the driver's seat for home-field advantage.

Here are three observations from a signature performance on an international stage.

If Purdy came to Mexico City needing a signature game to make his case for NFL MVP, he can probably put the pen away now.

The 49ers quarterback completed 21 of 26 passes for 255 yards and three touchdowns Sunday night against the Vikings. No interceptions. A 146.0 passer rating.

Against a defense considered the best in the NFL.

And in a game with huge playoff implications.

Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers looks to pass against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City, Mexico, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Getty Images

Maybe it's time to ask the question a different way: Who's got a better case than Purdy?

Joe Burrow certainly gets a say. Coming into Sunday, Burrow was the only quarterback ahead of Purdy in both QBR and passer rating. So this was hardly a quarterback playing catch-up in November, hoping a big performance on national television might get him invited into the conversation.

What he did Sunday ought to move him to the front of it.

Consider the assignment. Minnesota was allowing a league-low 14 points per game, with Brian Flores calling the kind of defense that can make a quarterback change his mind twice before the snap. And then regret both decisions by the time the play started.

Purdy threw nearly as many touchdown passes as incompletions. Three trips to the end zone. Five misses.

And for anyone inclined to give Kyle Shanahan the credit, by all means, give the man his due. It was a pretty good idea to get Mike Evans involved early. It was Purdy who put the ball on him five times for 91 yards before halftime and six for 106 overall.

Then there's the matter of what these games mean. The Rams, Seahawks and Vikings all have designs on representing the NFC in the Super Bowl. Purdy's 49ers have beaten all three, and Sunday night he was the best player on the field for the best team in football.

San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey (23) celebrates a touchdown with Mike Evans (5) during a game in Mexico City, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. AP Photo/Fernando Llano

The 49ers are 9-1. Seven games to go. Plenty of time for Burrow or somebody else to change the argument.

The 49ers keep answering the bell. Three big fights against three of the best teams in the NFC, and if you had the Rams, Seahawks or Vikings ahead on your scorecard, you're going to have to explain which round you were watching.

Three fights. Three decisive wins. And if any of those teams wants another crack at San Francisco in January, it might want to check the price of a flight to San Jose.

That's what was at stake Sunday night in Mexico City. The Rams and Seahawks are chasing the 49ers in the NFC West. The Vikings are chasing them for home-field advantage. At 9-1, with seven games to play, San Francisco holds the keys to two January parties in Santa Clara, the second of which would send somebody to the Super Bowl.

Anybody care to volunteer to be the visiting team?

San Francisco 49ers' Christian McCaffrey celebrates a touchdown against the Minnesota Vikings in Mexico City, Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. JOSE MENDEZ/EPA/Shutterstock

The Bears and Lions could have something to say about that. And even if the Rams and Seahawks no longer have a legitimate shot — barring a 49ers collapse, that is — they can play spoilers by tripping the 49ers up and muddying their path to the top seed in the NFC.

The Seahawks get that chance next week in Seattle.

Consider what happened to Minnesota. The Vikings arrived giving up a league-low 14 points a game. Shanahan and Purdy put three touchdowns on that defense before halftime. Evans caught five passes for 91 yards by the break, which gives you some idea of the price of keeping an eye on Christian McCaffrey.

And when Kirk Cousins got the ball back with a chance to make a game of it, 49ers safety Ji'Ayir Brown took it off his hands and went 18 yards the other way. Suddenly it was 28-10, and Brian Flores could have pitched a second-half shutout and still needed three scores from his offense.

That's the case for the 49ers as the NFC's most complete team. Spend your week figuring out what to do about Purdy, Evans and McCaffrey. Then hand the ball to your quarterback and wish him luck with Fred Warner and Nick Bosa.

The Rams, Seahawks and Vikings have all had their say. Anybody else?

It's getting interesting in the Bay Area.

The Vikings brought a defense to Mexico City that was giving up a league-low 14 points per game. Through nine games, Flores and his crew had taken the souls of so many opponents, a few of them might have needed an exorcist.

The 49ers took a look at that 14 and doubled it.

Seven of those points belonged to safety Ji'Ayir Brown, who took a Kirk Cousins interception back 18 yards to make it 28-10. That still left Kyle Shanahan's offense with three touchdowns in two quarters against a defense that generally allows two in four.

And the 49ers pushed that total to 35 in the second half.

Defensive coordinator Brian Flores of the Minnesota Vikings looks on during a game against the Buffalo Bills in Minneapolis, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images

The part that should keep defensive coordinators up this week was how willing Shanahan was to go right at Flores. You can understand why a play caller might spend a week preparing for Minnesota and talk himself out of half his playbook by Sunday. What if Flores brings pressure off the edge? What if the guy who looks like he's coming drops out and somebody else comes free?

Shanahan had a question of his own. What if we make them cover Mike Evans?

Purdy found Evans five times for 91 yards before halftime. Think about that from Flores' perspective. All week long, the conversation was about what his pressure might do to Purdy. By the time Flores headed to the locker room, he had to figure out what to do about Purdy.

And say you decide at halftime that Evans has seen his last single coverage of the evening. Fine. Where's that extra defender coming from? Because if you're pulling a safety closer to the sideline, Shanahan gets to spend the second half figuring out what Christian McCaffrey might do with a little more room in the middle of the field.

The Vikings have a fantastic defense. Nine games of making professional quarterbacks look like they'd rather be somewhere else ought to settle that.

The 49ers have a better offense. And that should send a shiver down the spine of the rest of the NFL.

#2664. Jevón Holland on controversial Parker Washington call: "Shoutout Vegas"

Back when the NFL hated gambling, it feared that widespread legalized sports betting would prompt fans to think the fix is in. Although the league has done its best to ignore the fact that its fears were accurate, not everyone has gotten the memo.

Giants safety Jevón Holland went there on Sunday, regarding the decision that Jaguars receiver Parker Washington failed to catch what would have been a touchdown pass in the fourth quarter.

“The game’s over? That might have been a catch,” Holland said, via Ryan Dunleavy of the New York Post. “That was a hell of a play. When they called it out, I was like, ‘Alright.’ Shoutout Vegas, man. I don’t know.”

Holland was surely joke. On the topic of suggesting that something fishy was happening, however, the NFL may not have a sense of humor.

It’s precisely the kind of comment to which the tinfoil-hat crowd will cling. Even if Holland doesn’t mean it, those who want to think the fix is in will seize on the statement of evidence that the fix is in.

As we’ve said time and again, the fix isn’t in. However, the NFL needs to be far more concerned about that perception than it is.

#2659. Jazz vs Mavericks recap: A wild finish in Salt Lake City

It was looking like another depressing night for Jazz fans. The young Jazz were plagued with turnovers (20 by the end of the third quarter), Darryn Peterson was struggling from three again (he's 0 for his last 15), and more injuries started piling up with Jaxson Hayes leaving early and Keyonte George turning another ankle. And once again, the Jazz slowly watched the Mavericks' lead grow and grow to near-insurmountable odds.

Then Isaiah Collier came in, and it felt like the Jazz had thrown in the towel.

With the game seemingly over after the third quarter, Svi Mykhailiuk scored 23 points in the fourth quarter and went absolutely nuclear. For the game, Mykhailiuk had 39 points and shot 10/15 from three. With less than 10 seconds left, Isaiah Collier scored on a layup to tie the game. On a side note, it's great that Isaiah Collier also had a hand in this one. He's had a great attitude despite being benched, and deserves some credit for his energy and hustle.

Heartbreak ensued when Ace Bailey fouled Cooper Flagg with four seconds left in the game, and Flagg hit the free throws. Then, an inbounds play ended with Kyle Filipowski missing a three to finish.

Yes, it was a dissapointing end. And yes, it was depressing to see our young players struggle again on a night they probably should have done better. It was the back end of a back-to-back for the Mavericks, after all. But this felt like something that could carry over into the next game and the rest of the season. It probably built some confidence for the bench, or at least in Svi Mykhailiuk, and might be the thing that reminds the Jazz they can win these games even when things aren't looking good. At least that's what you hope.

If I'm Keyonte George or Darryn Peterson, I'm looking at what Svi Mykhailiuk did, and I'm learning from it. The reality is that Utah has had two truly explosive games this season, one from Brice Sensabaugh, and one from Svi Mykhailiuk. We've had some dominant nights from Keyonte George but haven't experienced consistent explosive play from the starting lineup. If there's one thing you hope for from this one, it's that the Jazz starting lineup can take the confidence Svi showed tonight and incorporate it into their own play.

Hey, it might even improve their turnover issue. Believing in their ability could mean that the other things fall into place more, we'll find out tomorrow when they take on the Lakers once again.

#2656. Sunday Night Football: 49ers move to 9-1 with dominant 35-10 victory over Vikings

Are the 49ers the best team in the league?

Sunday night’s victory over the Vikings makes for a great argument that they are.

San Francisco put together a dominant performance against Minnesota, coming away with a 35-10 victory in Mexico City.

The 49ers were impressive on both offense and defense, but the result from the former was particularly notable. It’s the first time Minnesota has allowed 30 points all year, with only two teams reaching 20 points prior to Sunday’s contest.

Quarterback Brock Purdy had an excellent night, finishing 21-of-26 for 255 yards with three touchdowns. Head coach Kyle Shanahan took him out of the game midway through the fourth quarter with the contest effectively decided.

George Kittle caught the first two touchdowns of the night, with Mike Evans catching Purdy’s third late in the second quarter. The 49ers then scored again on Ji’Ayir Brown’s pick-six off Kirk Cousins to hold a 28-10 lead at halftime.

Running back Christian McCaffrey added a 6-yard touchdown early in the fourth quarter to cap a 13-play, 98-yard drive that put the game out of reach.

McCaffrey finished with 49 yards on 12 carries with a TD. He also caught two passes for 13 yards.

Evans had six catches for 109 yards with a score, Keenan Allen caught three passes for 38 yards, and Kittle finished with three receptions for 34 yards with two TDs.

On the other side, Kirk Cousins was frustrated by the 49ers’ pressure throughout the game as the Vikings couldn’t get much going on offense. Cousins ended the matchup 26-of-38 for 235 yards with a pick. He was taken out late in the contest, as Carson Wentz came in for mop-up duty.

Justin Jefferson led the Vikings with 86 yards on seven catches.

It didn’t help that Minnesota was missing left tackle Christian Darrisaw for much of the contest. He suffered a shoulder injury in the second quarter and did not return.

The 49ers also lost an offensive lineman, as right tackle Colton McKivitz suffered a serious lower-leg injury in the first half. He was carted off in an air cast after players were visibly upset by the nature of his injury.

With the win, the 49ers move to 9-1 and are in the driver’s seat for the NFC’s No. 1 seed. They will host the division-rival Seahawks next Sunday afternoon.

The Vikings fall to 7-3 after starting the season 6-0, having lost three of their last four. They will be back at home in Week 12 to face the Falcons.

#2655. Karl-Anthony Towns dominates Pacers in return to push Knicks’ win streak to five

Karl-Anthony Towns returned from an illness to carry the surging Knicks.

The center dominated the Pacers on Sunday night, finishing with 30 points and 13 rebounds in a resounding 113-106 victory at Madison Square Garden.

It represented a fifth straight win for the Knicks (11-6), who pulled away in the third quarter because Towns caught fire.

New York Knicks guard Jose Alvarado (5) and center Karl-Anthony Towns (32) react after scoring against the Indiana Pacers on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Jason Szenes for NY Post

"I just wanted to be aggressive and try to put this team in a position to win," Towns said.

He scored 16 points in just nine minutes of the period — including 12 in less than two minutes — as the Knicks went on a 20-11 run to take an 89-78 lead entering the fourth quarter.It ended with a nifty dribbling display into a 3-point conversion from Jose Alvarado.

Josh Hart helped close the win in the fourth quarter, earning a triple-double with 10 points, 11 boards and 10 assists in 39 minutes. Hart, who holds the franchise's single-season triple-double record, needed the confidence boost after riding the struggle bus to start the season.

Towns, meanwhile, has been consistently excellent.

A night earlier in a nail-biting victory over the Blazers, he was a DNP with an illness. Towns was then listed as questionable before Sunday's game, with coach Mike Brown claiming about 90 minutes before tipoff that Towns' availability was a game-time decision.

Josh Hart #3 and Jose Alvarado #5 of the New York Knicks react during a game against the Indiana Pacers on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, in New York. Getty Images

"I got out of bed," Towns said, "and played the game."

Luckily, Hart and Jalen Brunson (22 points, seven assists) picked up the slack to put away the plucky Pacers (5-12), who stink again this season but always play tougher — and more motivated — against the Knicks.

Towns, 31, is giving the Knicks plenty of reasons to reopen negotiations on a contract extension. He has 16 double-doubles in 16 appearances.

"Shoutout to the coach for trusting me more and more every day. And hearing me out," Towns said. "I'm appreciative of the trust this team has in me and the coaching staff has in me."

The Pacers were playing without Tyrese Haliburton, who has been out since last month with a hamstring strain. That didn't matter 10 days prior, when the Pacers toppled the Knicks in Indiana without Haliburton.

This time, the Knicks were home and better.

The Knicks had their own injury issues Sunday. OG Anunoby missed his second consecutive game with soreness, though Brown downplayed the severity of the injury. Miles McBride was a late scratch with left adductor tightness, a new injury that's concerning only because of the area: He missed time last season after sports hernia surgery, which is in the vicinity of his adductor.

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) shoots during the first half of a game against the Indiana Pacers on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026, at MetLife Stadium. Jason Szenes for NY Post

The first half was tight throughout, with neither team leading by more than four points and the score a modest 55-51, Knicks advantage, at the half. It was a continuation of New York's offense this season being behind the defense, which is apparently a league-wide trend since scoring is down across the NBA.

"I didn't know it was down overall," Brown said. "I don't know. I don't know if the defenses are getting better. I do know we, just our team, we haven't shot the ball as well as we'd like. But every game we're getting a little bit better, everybody's percentages are going up just a little bit every game, and that's exciting. I think eventually for us, right now our defense is way ahead of our offense, but our offense is coming, and hopefully we'll get there sooner than later."

Towns changed the tenor in the third quarter by hitting 5 of 8 shots, including 2-for-2 from beyond the arc. His return meant a DNP for James Wiseman, who played well in Saturday's win over the Blazers but is still the third-stringer behind Towns and Andre Drummond.

Landry Shamet, whom Brown declared pregame as the clear front-runner for Sixth Man of the Year, started again because of Anunoby's injury. He finished with 17 points in 32 minutes, including 12 points in the first half.

Hart looked like he was headed toward another frustrating night, appearing hesitant or even unwilling to take open 3-pointers. He had just two points at the half. But he picked up some momentum after the break, with the help of podcast buddy Brunson.

Early in the third quarter, the two were running together on a breakaway and Brunson, who had the open lane, bounced a pass to Hart for his first dunk of the season. It gave the Knicks a 12-point lead — their biggest of the night up to that point.

#2654. Fantasy Football: George Kittle, 49ers offense win the day versus Vikings' league-best defense

I've been married for almost 20 years, and you'd think I'd be used to things changing in an instant. I mean, I've had plenty of practice. Just last Friday, my evening plans switched from nothing (my default choice) to my wife inviting a couple over for board games, to her going to play cards with her sisters. It did turn out to be a quiet night for me. But it reminded me that in our house, a plan is, well, more of a suggestion.

I should've remembered that lesson as we headed into Sunday. From the kickoff to the early games, Week 11 reminded me how quickly things can flip in just a week. Honestly, I came away with more questions than answers. Let's dig into the storylines on some of the things that changed the most.

Before SNF, nobody wanted their QB to face the Vikings. The only passer to throw for multiple TDs was Jordan Love back in Week 1. Jared Goff in Week 8 was the first to complete over 70% of his passes against Minnesota's defense. And for TEs specifically, Keleki Latu was the sole player at his position to score against DC Brian Flores' unit.

Brock Purdy and George Kittle raised the bar in Mexico City.

Of course, the Vikings came in with their usual approach. Purdy saw five or more rushes on 73.3% of his passing attempts. That didn't matter. One, the blitzes only got home once. And two, only one incompletion was the result. Eight of his 10 completed passes turned into a first down or a score. Kittle was the primary fantasy beneficiary of Minnesota opting to treat Purdy like every other QB. But the rest of the receiver corps chipped in, too.

Target Rate: 26.9% (Evans), 15.4% (Samuel), 15.4% (Allen)

The "Unc Bowl" was in full effect for HC Kyle Shanahan. None of his aged WRs ran more than 50% of the snaps. But when they were out there, you knew where the ball was going. But the Vikings' secondary couldn't stop them. All four of the 30-plus-year-old pass-catchers were responsible for at least one explosive play. Only Christian McCaffrey got left out in the cold (he still found his way to the end zone). Minnesota's defense looked mortal for the first time all season.

But the state of the offense is a bigger issue.

Passing Success Rate: 43.6% (Week 11), 47.1% (Week 10)

After a confidence-building week against the Packers with Kirk Cousins fresh off the trade, everything came to a halt against San Francisco. Aaron Jones Sr. and Jordan Mason combined for a 35.3% rushing success rate on early downs, leaving Cousins with 8.6 yards to go in obvious passing situations. Justin Jefferson lost a fumble on a play where he (maybe?) would've scored if he hadn't changed directions. Cousins threw a pick-six. That's two possessions that could've tightened up the score. But as the Vikings were trying to catch up, an old fantasy option returned.

T.J. Hockenson came back to a part-time role after missing Week 10 with wrist and chest injuries. However, despite running the fewest routes of any of the starting pass-catchers, only Tai Felton had more targets. Hockenson should be in starting TE slots moving forward. But for Felton, I'd be more wary. The team opted not to place Jordan Addison on injured reserve, expressing optimism that he can be out on the field sooner than the IR designation. So, unless you're in dire need of a receiver, Hockenson should be the only addition from the Vikings off waivers as we head into Week 12.

Let's review Sunday's expectations for the Bears. The Saints' run defense came into the game allowing the 10th-most yards per game on the ground over their last six contests. Quinshon Judkins was the only starting RB to face New Orleans and exit with single-digit PPR points. HC Ben Johnson not only had Kyle Monangai returning from injury, but also the bye to plan.

Even in the first half, the results were concerning.

The Bears' approach to play-calling to start the game was simple: let's establish the run. D'Andre Swift touched the ball on the first four plays. Five of the nine plays on their opening drive were runs. Chicago finished the day with an -8.8% PROE (a season-low mark). Said another way, the volume was there. But Johnson split the pie up a few ways.

Swift: 48.0% (Early-Down Touch Rate), 37.0% (Route Share), 53.8%(RZ Snap Rate)

Swift and Monangai swapped series throughout most of the contest. Luckily for gamers rostering Swift, it was No. 4 who was on the field for Chicago's first TD drive after CJ Donaldson fumbled on their side of the field. Swift got the lone touch from inside the 10-yard line and converted for the score. But therein lies the problem. The combination of a healthy Ben Johnson running game and (theoretically) poor resistance from New Orleans should've garnered more production from anyone carrying the rock. Instead, we got the opposite.

Credit to the Saints' defensive line. They met the trio of Bears' rushers at or behind the LoS on 51.9% of their attempts. Monangai wasn't known for being the shiftiest of runners (0.0% forced missed tackle rate), but averaging 1.9 yards after contact didn't help. Swift took all of the short-yardage totes and only came out with one conversion on three attempts. And to make matters worse, Salvon Ahmed mixed in on early downs, siphoning yards away from both.

I could use the Bears' quick turnaround to face the Lions on Thursday to explain Ahmed's usage. However, season-lows in efficiency, leading to Caleb Williams' third-down environment getting more chaotic (fourth-highest average distance to convert), aren't just about the rotation. And after watching the Lions keep the Bucs' ground game in check, the Bears will need to adjust their run game in order to stay in the race for the top spot in the NFC North.

I understood Pittsburgh coming out flat against the Bengals in primetime last week. Don't get me wrong, I was surprised in the moment. But I've seen these games between division rivals before. I didn't expect to see the output continue a week later.

Aaron Rodgers' scramble to close out the first quarter was the longest running play for the Steelers on Sunday. If you're rostering Jaylen Warren, apologies in advance. After enjoying the backfield to himself for a stretch, maintaining the starter role and putting up three RB1 finishes, Warren was becoming a staple of fantasy rosters. However, everything's taken a step back.

Rushing Success Rate: 54.6% (Weeks 1-8), 28.6% (Week 10), 22.2% (Week 11)

Adj. Yards After Contact per Att.: 4.97, 2.14, 2.67

Pittsburgh's biggest play-calling shift was in how often Rodgers dropped back to pass. After having a negative PROE for three straight games, the Steelers were up to +6.3% (fourth-highest on the season). Accordingly, Warren carried the ball just nine times (second-fewest in '26). Philadelphia held him to zero yards before contact on two-thirds of his carries and stuffed him on a third. But that's OK. With more passing, Warren's involvement as a receiver should've kept his fantasy value afloat. However, his QB was also still in a slump.

Pressure-to-Sack Ratio: 62.5%, Season-high

The worst part is that the Eagles largely left Rodgers alone. They blitzed him just once. And yet, Rodgers still hit his season-high of five sacks. But I can't blame him. DK Metcalf decided that fighting with the defense was more important than catching the ball. And sure, Germie Bernard earned 10 targets. But again, six of them were on throws of five air yards or less. Rodgers didn't regularly look for him on intermediate or deep throws until the second half.

The knee-jerk reaction from gamers might be to start Bernard in Week 12. Metcalf might incur a suspension. Rodgers has been more efficient targeting Bernard over Metcalf in multiple games. However, with the Broncos and Texans on their upcoming schedule, I'd keep everybody in black and gold on your bench.

My largest concern with Fernando Mendoza starting during this stretch of games for the Raiders was the absence of Brock Bowers. I realize neither he nor HC Klint Kubiak could plan for an injury. But the chasm between Bowers and the rest of the pass-catchers would put anyone in a tough spot. And having to face Denver, coming off its bye, without his de facto WR1 would be a challenge. However, I didn't give enough credence to the idea that Kubiak could prepare his QB to do more with less.

To be clear, it wasn't all pretty. The Raiders punted on their first three drives. Mendoza ended the first quarter with just one more completed pass than sacks taken. It wasn't until the half was winding down that Mendoza started to get into the flow. But if there were concerns about whether or not Kubiak was giving Mendoza answers to the defense's questions, the rookie alleviated some of them.

EPA per Dropback: -0.02 (Week 11), -0.18 (Week 10)

Instead of forcing the ball to the middle of the field without his best receiver, Mendoza looked to the perimeter. It was the ideal adjustment given the strengths of the skill players he had on hand. Plus, he's pretty good at it. Mendoza averaged 0.68 EPA per dropback with a 55.6% completion rate on boundary throws. But Mendoza wasn't just aggressive — he was decisive, averaging more throws under 2.6 seconds. Oh, I guess I buried the lede there. All of his TD throws were to the perimeter. And at least one of his target-earners shouldn't be a surprise.

Unfortunately, not much changed for Ashton Jeanty as a runner. Six of his 11 carries came with a defender in the backfield. Denver held him to three or fewer yards on 54.5% of his attempts. But Jeanty came into the game behind only Christian McCaffrey in YPRR and was fifth in YAC per reception. If there was going to be a way to get Mendoza comfortable with the offense, using Jeanty as a receiver was the right call. But there's one more pass-catcher who should be on our radar.

Jack Bech's routes and targets have gone up in three straight weeks. He led the team in looks after Bowers left in Week 10 and was just one shy of Tre Tucker's total in Denver. But with receiving aDOTs of 9.3 and 8.1, Bech won't have the same volatility as a downfield option like Tucker. So even with Bowers likely to return, Bech should be a speculative add if you have the bench space.

Talk about narratives changing in a week. Jacksonville made multiple additions to the defense before the trade deadline, needed the full four quarters to get by Tennessee but, on paper, looked like one of the favorites to get to the Super Bowl.

And then the Giants reminded them there are no easy matchups in the NFL.

To be fair, the signs were there for the Jaguars to face some problems on offense. Starting LT Anton Harrison tore his ACL in Week 5, and C Robert Hainsey missed this game with a knee sprain. Minor injuries to RT Cole Van Lanen and RG Ezra Cleveland only complicated the situation further. Coincidentally, the G-Men were second to the Vikings in blitz rate and ninth in sack rate over their last six games. The outcome was one of Lawrence's worst outings this season.

Completion Percentage Over Expected: -2.1%, 3rd-lowest

Jacksonville's issue wasn't just that Lawrence's protection kept breaking down, but how fast things deteriorated. DC Dennard Wilson had his unit getting to Lawrence in 2.5 seconds or faster on 12 of his dropbacks. That's four more than his previous season-high. Accordingly, Lawrence's average time to throw skyrocketed to 3.3 seconds. He started taking more shots downfield (12.1 passing aDOT). Of course, the Giants mounting a multi-score lead by the end of the first half prompted the aggression. But New York reducing them to a one-dimensional offense was the larger issue.

Rushing Success Rate (on early downs): 27.3%, Season-low

Distance to the Sticks (on third downs): 10.8, Season-high

Bhayshul Tuten entered the game with foot/ankle injuries, missed time earlier in the game and then left early with a limp. Meanwhile, Chris Rodriguez Jr. ran into a stacked box on every single one of his early-down rushing attempts. Without a running game, Jacksonville turned into a dropback passing unit.

Let's assume Tuten misses Week 12. Jacksonville has its rematch against the Titans. Rodriguez is healthy. He should be at or near the top of your waiver priority. But I'd be wary about expecting similar target totals for Jakobi Meyers (10) and Josh Cameron (7). Lawrence just attempted more than 45 passes for the first time since Week 7 of last season. Unless you think the Titans can do the same, the offense should go back to its balanced ways in Week 12.

#2652. Mohamed Diawara and Pacome Dadiet in tight battle for Knicks minutes that could last all season

Mohamed Diawara versus Pacôme Dadiet "will be a battle all year" for minutes, according to coach Mike Brown, who met with both players in preseason to warn them about the battle.

"It's gonna be a competition all year," Brown said, "and it's gonna be back and forth."

Dadiet was the winner this weekend for back-to-back victories over the Blazers and Pacers, combining for 28 minutes and 10 points.

Pacome Dadiet (4) of the New York Knicks misses a layup against Robert Williams III (35) of the Portland Trail Blazers in New York, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026. Getty Images

Diawara, meanwhile, combined for eight minutes and zero points in the two games, including a DNP in Saturday's nail-biting win over the Blazers.

It's a surprising development considering Diawara just signed a multiyear deal and Dadiet is in the final season of his contract because the Knicks didn't pick up his option. The expectation is that this is Dadiet's last campaign in New York.

Still, Brown explained Sunday he always wanted to give Dadiet a chance, even after assistant coach Brendan O'Connor suggested Diawara get the nod to start the season.

"I said the first opportunity I get, I'm gonna try to throw [Dadiet] in the game 'cause he's been playing well in practice and stuff like that," Brown said. "And it's just, in my opinion, his turn … but it's not permanent."

As a second-round rookie in 2025, Diawara was a surprise addition to the rotation last season while Dadiet, a 2024 first-round pick, was benched. It led to the Knicks giving Diawara a four-year, $11.2 million contract in the summer but obviously no guarantee of playing time.

New York Knicks forward Mohamed Diawara (51) shoots past Cleveland Cavaliers center Evan Mobley (4) on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

On Saturday, Brown even played two-way contract Dalton Knecht over Diawara — although that flipped Sunday with Knecht never getting off the bench.

Miles McBride was a late scratch to Sunday's game with a left adductor strain. OG Anunoby sat his second straight game with calf soreness, though Brown said it was a precautionary absence.

Knicks president Leon Rose will be inducted Monday into the New Jersey Jewish Sports Hall of Fame.

Rose, who started his professional career as an attorney in the Camden County Prosecutor's Office in 1988, is a South Jersey product who grew up in Cherry Hill and played basketball at Rutgers-Camden.

He then became a power agent at Creative Artists Agency while repping LeBron James, Allen Iverson, Chris Paul, Dwyane Wade and Jalen Brunson, among others. He has been leading the Knicks front office since 2020.

Rose will be inducted with Jess Holtz, the CAA agent who reps Karl-Anthony Towns, former Rutgers basketball player Jeffrey Kleinbaum and Rob Kaminsky, the left-handed pitcher for the L.A. Angels.

#2651. Brewers bash champion Dodgers to brink of NLCS sweep; CBS Sports Preseason All-America team revealed

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2650. ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’ review: Defense rules as Giants defeat Jacksonville

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants didn't do it the easy way, but they did manage to get a huge victory over the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. Let's get to our 'Kudos and Wet Willies' review.

The defense as a whole — The Giants turned away the Jaguars again and again on Sunday, refusing to let a missed field, a Cam Skattebo fumble, and an inconsistent day from quarterback J.J. McCarthy stand in the way of a signature victory for the Giants as they improved to 6-3-1, and moved a step closer to their first NFC East title since 2011.

The Giants pressured a flustered Jacksonville quarterback Trevor Lawrence into his worst game of the season. Lawrence went 25 of 47 for 301 passing yards, but threw two interceptions, was sacked three times, hit 11 times, adn was chased endlessly by Giants pass rushers.

The Giants got interceptions from Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo. They had 14 passes defensed. They had a key fourth-down stop on fourth-and-1 at the Giants' 11-yard line late in the third quarter after a Cam Skattebo fumble had given the Jaguars the ball at the New York 31-yard line.

Abdul Carter — Flush with the excitement of a great performance in a huge victory for the Giants, Carter called himself "the best in the world."

Carter has a long way to go before he can prove that, but he might well have been the best pass rusher in the NFL on Sunday. Carter said he played "real angry" after seeing some online criticism over the fact that he entered the game with just 2.0 sacks.

Lawrence ended up feeling Carter's anger in the second-year edge defender's best game as a pro. Carter had two sacks, five quarterback hits, and a career-high 12 pressures, per NextGen Stats. This was the first multi-sack game of Carter's career.

Deonte Banks — Banks set up the Giants' first points with an interception that put the ball at the Jacksonville 31-yard line. He also had three passes defensed, including one on a desperation throw into the end zone by Lawrence on a fourth-quarter pass from the 12-yard line.

Paulson Adebo — The forgotten veteran cornerback was forced into action when the Giants lost starter Greg Newsome II to an ankle injury after just four snaps. Adebo was terrific.

Adebo intercepted a Lawrence pass with 11:08 left in the game, putting the Giants at the Jacksonville 28-yard line and setting up a Dominic Zvada field goal. Adebo also had four passes defensed. Per Pro Football Focus, he gave up just one completion in eight targets while spending much of his day chasing Jacksonville's Parker Washington.

Per PFF, his passer rating against was 0.0. Adebo got a game ball from John Harbaugh.

D.J. Reader — The big nose tackle's job is to stuff the run. He certainly did that Sunday with a tackle for loss and, per PFF, three stops. Somebody forgot to tell him, though, that nose tackles not named Dexter Lawrence aren't supposed to be impact pass rushers. Reader had a sack, two quarterback hits, and five total pressures. He continued to play at a Pro Bowl level.

Reader celebrated with a simple social media post:

Malik Nabers — I am honestly not sure about this one, but Nabers did have seven receptions for 55 yards and a touchdown. Through 29 career games, Nabers has caught 192 passes, the third-most through that many games in NFL history behind only Odell Beckham Jr. (199) and Puka Nacua (194).

Xavier Gipson — The Giants' new return man averaged 25.0 yards on five kickoff returns, including a 36-yarder, and had a 27-yard punt return. The Giants said they signed Gipson off the Philadelphia Eagles' practice squad because they needed "a spark" in the return game. Gipson gave them one.

Dru Phillips — Yeah, yeah. Phillips gave up seven completions on nine targets. Don't care. I care about his three passes defensed, especially on fourth-and-1 from the Giants' 11-yard line in the third quarter.

Jordan Stout — The Giants' punter averaged 60.3 yards on four punts, with a net of 54.5. The shortest punt Stout had was 57 yards. The amazing thing is that Stout manages to hit the ball that far while still getting enough hang time on his punts to give the Giants a chance to cover them.

Zaire Barnes and Tyler Nubin — Barnes had four special teams tackles, added to the league-leading 14 he had entering the game. Nubin has not sulked about losing his starting safety job to Ar'Darius Washington. He had three special teams tackles.

Second half offense — The Giants' offense seemed out of sorts after Cam Skattebo's fumble late in the third quarter with the Giants seemingly driving for what could have been a score that would have effectively put the game out of reach.

After that the Giants got just one first down over their next four possessions, netting -20 yards of offense along the way. They played oddly for a team trying to run the clock and protect a lead. Over those four drives, they ran the ball only one time. Those four possessions took a total of just 3:44 off the clock, and continued to give Jacksonville opportunities to get back into the game.

Micah McFadden — This was a rough night for McFadden. He made six tackles, and missed same number. Missed tackles have always been a bug-a-boo for McFadden, and this might have been his worst-ever game in that department. He missed a tackle in the backfield on a fourth-and-1 that went for a 21-yard run, and had a handful of chances to nab Lawrence in the backfield that he could not convert.

Cam Skattebo — Skattebo had a costly third-quarter fumble. He had just 34 yards on 14 carries, an average of 2.4 yards per attempt. After his third quarter fumble, the Giants seemed determined NOT to hand him the ball. Still, when the Giants needed a first down to ice the game, Skattebo delivered with two runs for 10 yards and a game-clinching first down at the two-minute mark.

Skattebo also delivered a trademark backflip, a move he said he had retired, after the victory-sealing first down.

"When energy calls for it, it calls for it," Skattebo said. "I do whatever I can to bring the energy for the team. I play this game with my heart and soul. When that happens it's second nature. It's hard to hold back from."

J.J. McCarthy — This was not McCarthy's steadiest game throwing the ball. He went just 18 of 38 (47.4%) for 173 yards and a touchdown.

McCarthy overshot a wide open Darnell Mooney on a couple of deep throws. He missed Mooney on a deep out where he was open. He failed to see an open Malik Nabers for what could have been a long touchdown.

Yet, he made game-winning plays. His 8-yard touchdown pass to Nabers was a nice touch throw. He made a terrific 19-yard throw to Malachi Fields for a critical first down inside the three-minute mark. McCarthy used his legs to escape the pocket and pick up some key first downs.

His play of the game, though, might have been his touchdown-saving tackle of Antonio Johnson after the Skattebo fumble.

Dominic Zvada — The rollercoaster ride with the Giants' strong-legged rookie placekicker continued on Sunday. He made field goals of 53 and 54 yards — from the right hash mark where all six of his misses had occurred this season. Then, Zvada missed a chip shot 32-yarder from that right hash early in the third quarter before adding a 43-yarder from the left hash mark for three critical points with 10:03 to play.

The Giants continue to express faith in Zvada, but it can't be a surprise to anyone if the Giants work out placekickers some time soon.

#2647. Jayson Tatum misses game winner in loss to Warriors as Celtics continue on worst losing skid since 2021

The Boston Celtics, thanks to a big defensive stand from Draymond Green late, are now on their worst losing skid in years.

The Celtics fell to the Golden State Warriors 88-87 on Sunday night at the Chase Center in San Francisco. That was Boston's fourth straight loss, too, which marked the first time the franchise had lost four consecutive games since May 2021.

They had gone a ridiculous 429 games without a four-game losing skid, which was the second-longest stretch in franchise history. The Celtics once went 468 games from 1962-68.

Boston led by as many as 11 late in the third quarter, and seemed in a great spot to grab the win and limit the damage to three losses. But the Warriors slowly chipped away and got back into the game, and even took the lead on a huge Brandin Podziemski 3-pointer with about 2:30 left in the contest. Those were the last points that the Warriors scored.

But with just eight seconds left, Tatum had a great look to win the game. Down by a single point, Tatum drove at Green and took a fadeaway jumper from the elbow over Green. The shot was off the mark, and he finished going 0 of 7 from the field in the second half.

Podziemski led the Warriors with 18 points and seven rebounds in the win, which moved them to 9-8 on the season and ended a five-game losing streak of their own. Charles Bassey added 13 points and nine rebounds, and Green finished with nine points. The Warriors are still missing Stephen Curry, who is sidelined with an abdominal injury.

Tatum finished with 27 points and 10 rebounds while shooting 8 of 20 from the field. Derrick White had 14 points, and Luka Garza added 10 off the bench. They were the only three Celtics players to hit double figures, and the 87 points they managed as a team were the fewest they've scored all season.

It wasn't just Sunday night where they blew a lead, either. Boston had double-digit leads in three of their four losses, including a 17-point lead over the Denver Nuggets before blowing that contest on Wednesday. They were up by 13 points at Sacramento on Saturday, too, before Keegan Murray sank a put-back jumper to seal the one-point win.

Boston got the losing streak started on Monday in a 10-point loss to the Orlando Magic, who rallied late to grab the win at TD Garden.

While the losing streak isn't great, it's far from the time to be concerned for the Celtics. It's not even December yet, and they sit at 11-6 on the season. That's good for third in the Eastern Conference standings, behind only the Philadelphia 76ers and Atlanta Hawks. There is plenty of time for the Celtics to rebound from this stretch and maintain their position in the East. And, the longest losing streak in NBA history is 28 games. The Celtics aren't even close to that mark.

But their run of keeping losing streaks to a minimum has officially come to an end. They'll have a chance to snap the four-game losing skid Tuesday night against the Washington Wizards.
