#2640. What NFL had to say about controversial call that took critical touchdown from Jaguars in loss to Giants

The football world is abuzz over the no-touchdown call on a fourth–quarter pass to Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington in Sunday's game against the Giants.

While it appeared that Washington had made the catch in the end zone with the Jaguars trailing the Giants 20-6 at the time, the officials ruled it an incomplete pass and confirmed the call after a video review.

The Giants went on to win the game 23-18.

New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips (22) defends against Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) on Nov. 22, 2026, in Brooklyn, N.Y. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

Everyone from Washington to the fans to CBS Sports rules analyst Gene Steratore all believed that Washington had control of the ball.

"I did not think he lost possession of the football. … I think it's a touchdown, fellas," Steratore said during the broadcast.

However, the NFL did not agree. In an interview with a pool reporter, NFL VP of instant replay Mark Butterworth said Washington did not have full control of the ball.

"The ruling on the field was an incomplete pass," Butterworth said. "First, to overturn a call, we need clear and obvious video evidence to overturn the on-field ruling. It was determined that the receiver did not gain full control of the ball until he was out of bounds."

In follow-up questions, he confirmed that he was referring to the fact that when Washington hit the ground, the ball was moving in the Jaguars receiver's hands.

Jaguars head coach Liam Coen told reporters after the game that the explanation he got was that "the ball switched hands, so that's what it came down to."

New York Giants cornerback Dru Phillips (22) defends Jacksonville Jaguars wide receiver Parker Washington (11) during a game on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Corey Sipkin for the NY POST

Jacksonville had to settle for a field goal on the drive to only cut the Giants' lead to 20-9.

"I felt good about it, but they said it wasn't a catch, so had to move on and finish that game," Washington told reporters after the game.

#2638. MLB rumors: Blue Jays targeting Ketel Marte, Giants rejecting trade calls for ace Logan Webb

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The annual GM Meetings came and went this week with two significant transactions. The Braves signed reliever Evan Phillips (three years and $35 million) and the Red Sox signed slugger Jake Bauers (four years and $58 million). Bauers will give Boston some sorely needed home run power. Phillips will pair with Robert Suarez in the late innings for Atlanta.

Otherwise, the GM Meetings brought a lot of rumors and presumably the groundwork was laid for moves that could be completed later this offseason. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Saturday's hot stove happenings.

The Blue Jays have interest in Diamondbacks second baseman Ketel Marte, who has a full no-trade protection, reports Sportsnet. It does not appear a trade is imminent. We ranked Marte among the offseason's top trade candidates despite his odd AWOL incidents the last few seasons. Even at 33, he remains one of the game's best second basemen.

The Blue Jays went 79-83 this past season largely because of their offense, which ranked dead last in runs and home runs. They also ranked 17th in WAR at second base as All-Star Ernie Clement ran out of steam in the second half. Offensively, Marte is coming off his worst 162-game season since 2018, though he would still represent a clear upgrade for the Blue Jays.

The Giants continue to decline trade calls about ace righty Logan Webb, reports USA Today. Webb, 30 next week, had his worst full season in the big leagues in 2026, in part due to a nagging knee injury, though he is signed affordably through 2028. San Francisco needs to add to its rotation, not subtract one of the game's best and most durable starters.

That said, a Webb trade would presumably net the Giants multiple young players and improve the team's talent base. It never hurts to listen, but for now, the Giants seem disinclined to move their best pitcher since Madison Bumgarner was in his prime. Webb and Landen Roupp are the only locks for San Francisco's 2027 rotation at the moment.

Not surprisingly, the Braves want to add at least one starting pitcher, according to The Athletic. They could also re-sign Raisel Iglesias or bring in another late-inning reliever even after signing Phillips. Chris Sale and Grant Holmes are Atlanta's only returning healthy starters. Bryce Elder (knee), Spencer Schwellenbach (elbow) and Spencer Strider (elbow) all finished the season injured.

The Braves will give Didier Fuentes, who was so dominant as a reliever this past season, a chance to start in 2027. It will be difficult to count on him for a full season, however. Fuentes, 21, threw a career-high 97 innings between the minors, majors, and postseason in 2026. Atlanta will need to monitor his workload next year. Another starter to soak up innings is a must this offseason.

The Tigers have interest in free agent left-hander Shota Imanaga, reports MLB.com. Jackson Jobe, Troy Melton, River Ryan, and Framber Valdez are presumably locks for Detroit's rotation. Ty Madden and Keider Montero are depth options. Reese Olson is expected back from shoulder surgery early next year. Still, the Tigers could clearly use another starting pitcher.

We ranked Imanaga, 33, as the 30th-best free agent available this offseason. He has been very home run prone the last two years (1.9 homers per nine innings), which could make him a good match for what is now called Fifth Third Park. Detroit's stadium tends to play pitcher-friendly, particularly in April and September (and October), when the ball doesn't carry well in the cold.

The Blue Jays are receiving calls about infielder Ernie Clement and utility man Davis Schneider, reports The Athletic. Teams have also inquired about catcher Brandon Valenzuela, who was a Gold Glove finalist as a rookie in 2026. Toronto reportedly has interest in Jazz Chisholm Jr. as it seeks more of a power bat on the infield, potentially making Clement expendable.

Schneider, 27, had a poor 2026 and spent time in Triple-A, though he is versatile and has hit lefties in spots over the years. There is a shocking shortage of quality right-handed bats throughout baseball right now. Schneider's heavy plate discipline approach and ability to play left field as well as some infield positions make him an interesting enough target this offseason.

The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox are among several teams pursuing Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Taira, 26, had a 1.36 ERA in 145 innings for the Seibu Lions in 2026. We ranked him as the 19th-best free agent available this offseason, though he could ultimately wind up in the bullpen given his height (5-foot-8).

The Padres and two Chicago teams need starting pitching this offseason (they need multiple starters, really) and would likely use Taira in their rotation, at least to begin the season. For what it's worth, Taira told Sanspo he does not have a preferred destination, geographically. The Cubs, Padres, and White Sox would all give him a chance to pitch for a contender right away.

The Cardinals have declined trade inquiries into first baseman Alec Burleson and shortstop Masyn Winn, according to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. St. Louis is also receiving interest in catchers Jimmy Crooks and Pedro Pagés, who are more likely to be traded. Burleson and Winn are off-limits, though, and considered part of the long-term future in St. Louis.

Leo Bernal, who was so impressive during his September call up, and top prospect Rainiel Rodriguez are the future behind the plate for the Cardinals. Pagés is a traditional glove-first backup catcher. Crooks has some offensive upside thanks to his hard-hit ability (exit velocity, etc.), and he rates well as a pitch-framer and thrower. He's an appealing target for catcher-needy teams.

#2635. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2634. What's next for Red Sox after Jake Bauers deal? Plus more intel from the MLB GM Meetings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LAS VEGAS — Uncertainty permeated the ARIA Resort & Casino throughout this week's MLB GM Meetings. The looming lockout, of course, played a major role in all of this.

With Dec. 1  approaching, media, executives, and all within the baseball industry had some questions: what would baseball look like once the inevitable lockout goes into place? What will it look like once it returns? How do you build a roster with such indeterminacy?

For the Red Sox, a small piece of this peculiar period centers on what to do with former top prospect Kristian Campbell.

Tuesday (Nov. 17) is a significant date, marking the deadline for teams to decide which players to protect from the Rule 5 draft by adding them to their 40-man roster. Campbell, who did not appear in a big-league game in 2026, is currently on the 40-man, signing an eight-year $60 million extension just eight games into his 2025 rookie campaign. But after his demotion in late June of that season, Campbell never found his way back to the majors.

Now, with the lockout upon baseball, according to one source familiar with the situation, Campbell's 40-man spot might be in jeopardy.

Boston is weighing the possibility of designating Campbell for assignment. When Craig Breslow, the Sox's president of baseball operations, was asked about that Tuesday, he brushed aside the question.

"I'm not going to speak to that right now," he said "Kristian's part of our organization. We're really happy about that, and we are invested in doing everything we can to get him to perform like he's capable of."

Now, if the Red Sox do DFA Campbell, the belief is that he would clear waivers, given his contract and lackluster performance at the minor-league level. Campbell is owed $55 million over the next six seasons, earning $13 million and $16 million over the 2031 and 2032 seasons, respectively. Campbell posted a .256/.383/.380 slash line with eight homers in 462 plate appearances at Triple-A in 2026.

Because of those figures, one league executive suggested during the GM Meetings that their club would have no interest in Campbell. The exec took it a step further, confidently suggesting that they couldn't envision any team claiming the outfielder, considering the contract.

Hypothetically, if Campbell is DFA'd, the Red Sox would free up a 40-man roster spot. If he clears waivers, Campbell, who has less than a year of MLB service time, would be outrighted to Triple-A Worcester. The Red Sox could then eventually add him back to the 40-man roster once they feel his production is worthy of another promotion to the parent club.

None of this would provide the Red Sox with any financial relief unless another team were to claim him. Campbell's contract would still count toward their competitive balance tax payroll even if he were removed from the 40-man roster and remained in the minors.

The risk-reward of such a move is something the Red Sox will also have to consider. Campbell has already acknowledged losing confidence following his recent struggles at both the major- and minor-league levels.

"He's got a world of potential," said Breslow. "We saw it in the minor leagues when he was coming up. We saw it in the first part of the season in [2025]. Then I think we started to see it in the second half last year, too, [at Worcester]. I still feel like he has a really bright big-league career ahead of him, and excited to get into spring training and see that manifest on the field."

The Red Sox signed Jake Bauers to a four-year, $58 million deal Friday, giving the club another power bat in their lineup. Willson Contreras will continue to anchor first base while Bauers will serve as the primary DH, filling in for Contreras from time to time.

Bauers had a breakout season with the Brewers this year, batting .266/.389/.484 with an .874 OPS and 26 homers. The combo of plate discipline and damage in the strike zone intrigued the Red Sox. Furthermore, his ability to lift the ball in the air and use the entire field despite being a lefty gives the Red Sox confidence that he will be productive at Fenway.

With Bauers part of the fold, though, Jarren Duran's future with the club is even more murky. The Sox are a heavily left-handed offensive club with Bauers, Wilyer Abreu, Masataka Yoshida, Roman Anthony, and Duran in the mix.

One is likely going to have to go. And Duran, who could earn upwards of $11 million in arbitration next season, appears to be the most likely to be dealt.

Even before the Bauers signing, multiple sources suggested during the GM Meetings that both the Red Sox and Duran might be better off parting ways via trade.

"I've been hearing for three years now about the outfield logjam that we have, but the reality is we haven't had all of our outfielders, including Masataka, healthy at the same time," Breslow said. "These things have largely taken care of themselves, unfortunately."

#2632. MVP Brock Purdy? 49ers next Super Bowl champions? It's all on the table now for San Francisco

For millennia, philosophers and professors have pondered an impossible question: What happens when an irresistible force meets an immovable object? Well, we have our answer, and we didn't even need AI to solve it: Irresistible Force knocks out Immovable Object by 25 points.

San Francisco and Minnesota arrived in Mexico City at the absolute pinnacles of the NFL's two barometers of excellence. No team in the NFL gains more yards per play than the 49ers. No team sacks quarterbacks more than Minnesota. Dominating offense, smothering defense. Irresistible force, immovable object.

The 49ers strode onto the field at Estadio Azteca and proceeded to stomp all over the Vikings. San Francisco set the tone with an opening seven-play, 72-yard drive that finished in the end zone less than four minutes. The Vikings immediately struck back with a touchdown.

And then, like a street fighter wiping a drop of blood off his lip before administering a generational beatdown, the 49ers blew away the league's top scoring defense with a total of 35 points, through the air and on the ground. And if you could score touchdowns by water, well, the 49ers probably would have done that too. This was a statement win carved into the side of a mountain, a declaration that the road to the Super Bowl runs through San Francisco.

At 9-1, the 49ers lead the the NFC West by three games and the NFC as a whole by a game, and stand even with the Bills for the best record in the NFL. Aside from an inexplicable loss to the Falcons — who probably won't get another shot at the 49ers this season — San Francisco has overwhelmed its opposition at every turn.

If there's anything that can slow this 49ers team, it's the blue medical tent. Injuries have ravaged the 49ers all season, and on Sunday night, San Francisco ran out a Geriatric Avengers of thirtysomethings including George Kittle, Mike Evans, Christian McCaffrey, Deebo Samuel Sr. and Kyle Juszczyk. All that experience gives the 49ers a big-game-pressure edge that few teams can match, but it also makes them intensely vulnerable to injury. Stints on the IR are a when, not an if, for the 49ers. Right tackle Colton McKivitz was the latest as he suffered a gruesome leg injury in the first half Sunday night.

The guy ensuring all those uncs get the ball is finally receiving some attention of his own again, too. Brock Purdy hasn't shown up on MVP leaderboards since finishing fourth in his breakout season of 2023. This season ought to change that. He's among the league leaders in touchdowns, passer rating and completion percentage, among other useful stats.

Against the best defense in the NFL, all Purdy did was throw for three touchdowns and 255 yards on 21 of 26 completions. He's grown into the perfect weapon for head coach Kyle Shanahan's unorthodox offense, and Sunday was the perfect showcase.

"Brock, he didn't get rattled, which he really never does," Shanahan said after the game. "It's not like it's something new today to me with Brock. Brock's been like this since Day 1, and he's played at a very high level for a number of years now."

Purdy and Shanahan wisely used the Vikings' vicious aggressiveness against them. The NFL Next Gen Stats chart of Purdy's completions tells the tale; virtually all of his completions were within 10 yards of the line of scrimmage, meaning he got rid of the ball so quickly that Minnesota couldn't catch up. You can't record a sack when the ball's already downfield.

"He just has this aura in the huddle," said Kittle, who caught Purdy's first two touchdown passes. "Everybody locks eyes with him, and we know every play, we have the chance to do something special."

"He's the best player in the game right now. He's super dialed in, the way he prepares, the way he competes," said Evans, who caught Purdy's third touchdown pass of the night, late in the first half. "He's tough. I always thought he's been underrated — his precision. Super-smart player."

This 49ers team is something special, and not just because it has managed to win in three countries and two hemispheres this season. The Niners in the meat of their schedule now; the Seahawks, Rams and Chiefs all await over the next five weeks. So too do teams like the Chargers, Eagles and Cardinals; San Francisco's schedule ranks 23rd in the NFL in terms of remaining difficulty, per Tankathon.

"We're halfway through this year. We've done some good things, but I mean, [the Super Bowl is] still to be determined," Shanahan said. "We know how we've been so far, but we're halfway there and we've got a long way to go."

Shanahan has led his teams to within sight of the promised land, reaching the Super Bowl as a head coach or coordinator on three separate occasions. In all three, the Lombardi Trophy eluded him. There's no reason to expect that this season will be any different … except for the fact that there was no reason to expect San Francisco would throw around the best defense in the league, either. The Irresistible Force rolls on.

The Padres are in desperate need of starting pitching, should they wish to continue contending. The rotation right now would be Joe Musgrove, Randy Vásquez, JP Sears, Jhony Brito and a shrugging emoji. Sure enough, they are all over the rumor mill for rotation help.

The San Diego Union-Tribune reports that they've shown interest in "virtually every starting pitcher" in free agency, "from Tarik Skubal on down. Further, ESPN reports that the Padres have a meeting set up with Skubal but have also shown interest in Freddy Peralta, as well as Michael King, Nick Pivetta and Nick Martinez.

Expect them to remain active until they land at least two starters.

It's no secret that the Diamondbacks are open to trading All-Star second baseman Ketel Marte. The Blue Jays have been sniffing around, and now the Orioles have emerged as a suitor, per MLB.com.

Presumably, if they are able to swing a deal for Marte, there would be some shuffling with more trades and/or moving someone to the outfield.

The Mets could have an opening at first base as things currently stand and they've checked in on free agent Ty France, according to the New York Post.

Currently, the Mets are looking at Jared Young (coming off a scary head injury), Mark Vientos and Jorge Polanco as options at first base.

France, 32 and probably considered a journeyman at this point, had a big season in 2026 for the Padres. He hit .295/.363/.502 (139 OPS+) with 21 homers, 72 RBI and a career-high 4.5 WAR.

Reliever Jonathan Loáisiga is close to signing with a new team, reports ESPN. The Dodgers are among five teams involved, with the New York Post adding the Phillies, Mets, Yankees and Blue Jays to the mix.

In 67 outings last season for Arizona, Loáisiga pitched to a 2.42 ERA, 1.03 WHIP and had 48 strikeouts in 67 innings.

The Yankees have re-signed left-handed reliever Tim Hill to a one-year, $2.25 million deal with a $2.5 million club option for 2028, per ESPN. Hill, 36, made 67 appearances last season with a 4.60 ERA, 1.14 WHIP and 25 strikeouts in 58 ⅔ innings. He held lefties to a .213/.265/.346 line.

#2627. 10 most interesting MLB non-tender decisions, including a Red Sox staple and a former Rookie of the Year

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This Friday, Nov. 20, is an important date on MLB's offseason calendar. It is the deadline for teams to offer 2027 contracts to their arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players. The player does not have to sign by Friday's 5 p.m. ET deadline, but he must be offered a contract. If he's not, the player is considered non-tendered and immediately becomes a free agent.

Dozens of players are non-tendered every offseason when teams determine their production no longer warrants the salary. Adolis García, Nathaniel Lowe, Alek Manoah, and Christopher Morel were among the notable non-tenders last offseason. Go back a few years and big names like Cody Bellinger and Kyle Schwarber were non-tendered.

With that in mind, here are the 10 most interesting non-tender decisions ahead of Friday's deadline, using the arbitration salary projections at the indispensable MLB Trade Rumors. You can be sure these teams will scour the trade market for these players and try to get something back before making the non-tender official.

Projected salary: $11.1 million (team control through 2028)

Duran was a non-tender candidate even before the Jake Bauers signing pushed him out of the everyday lineup. There is no such thing as too many good players, but the Red Sox now have two first basemen (Bauers and Willson Contreras) and four outfielders (Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela). Mickey Gasper and Masataka Yoshida are still around too. That's eight players for five lineup spots (first base, DH, three outfield spots). On any given day, three of those guys will be on the bench. Duran, who got MVP votes in 2024, had a 20-20 season in 2026, but it came with a ballooning strikeout rate and a .266 on-base percentage. He has been on the trade block for close to two years now and the writing is on the wall. If the Red Sox are unable to trade Duran this week, there's a real chance he'll get non-tendered Friday given his hefty salary projection.

Projected salary: $7.7 million (team control through 2028)

Former No. 1 overall draft picks have been non-tendered in the past (Tim Beckham most recently), just not by the team that drafted them. Non-tendering Torkelson would be a tough look for the Tigers even though he has not developed into the impact hitter he was projected to be coming out of Arizona State. Simply put, the salary is beginning to outweigh the production. Torkelson, 27, is a 25-30 homer bat with one of the league's highest strikeout rates, middling on-base percentages, and no secondary value (defense, baserunning, etc.). That said, the Tigers do not have an obvious replacement first baseman ready to step in (Colt Keith was the backup in 2026). That, plus the fact that Torkelson has No. 1 pick pedigree, could keep him in Detroit another year.

Projected salary: $2.3 million (team control through 2029)

The American League Rookie of the Year in 2024, Gil has battled injuries and ineffectiveness in the two seasons since. The swing-and-miss rate on his fastball went from an elite 28.5% in 2024 to a below-average 18.8% in 2025 and 17.4% in 2026. Gil, 28, spent time in Triple-A this past season and the Yankees moved him into the bullpen late in the year, where the results were so-so. The salary projection is a pittance, particularly for a team with New York's payroll, though Gil is now out of minor-league options (he must pass through waivers to go to Triple-A) and doesn't have an obvious role. Because he is a pitcher and breathing, and also has a major award win in the not-too-distant past, the Yankees might be able to find a trade partner this week. If not, Gil is a definite non-tender candidate.

Projected salary: $7.6 million (team control through 2028)

A fan favorite and an All-Star this past season, Clement crashed hard in the second half, and the fact of the matter is he has a .295 on-base percentage in his three full seasons with the Blue Jays. Also, the soon-to-be 31-year-old's defensive numbers tumbled this year. Clement's contact skills are elite and he's a versatile, high-energy player. As a utility guy, he's an ace. As an everyday player, he's stretched. Clement's projected salary is hefty for a utility player, particularly one with limited offensive upside who no longer reliably catches the baseball. My guess is the Blue Jays will keep him and live with the salary, but it's not an obvious decision.

Projected salary: $5.1 million (team control through 2028)

Similar to Torkelson, non-tendering a former No. 1 overall pick would be a tough look for the Twins, but a clean break might be best for all involved at this point. Lewis, 27, has trended down since his boffo second half in 2023, enough that he was sent to Triple-A for a spell this summer. He's also moved down the defensive spectrum from third base to first base. It's not due to a lack of effort; Lewis is a major tinkerer who has tried all sorts of swing adjustments. It just hasn't come together. A fresh start elsewhere, away from the spotlight of former No. 1 pick and face of the franchise, might be best for him. The budget-conscious Twins could then reallocate the projected $5.1 million elsewhere on the roster. Right now, they can't count on Lewis to hit or have a meaningful impact defensively.

Projected salary: $3.4 million (team control through 2028)

In 2023, Gorman slugged 27 home runs and looked like one of baseball's top young power hitters. In the three seasons since, he has not come close to repeating that success. The hope was that moving him to third base, his natural position, would unlock Gorman's offense following the Nolan Arenado trade. That didn't happen, and Gorman spent a big chunk of the summer in Triple-A, where he continued to have a hard time making contact. Now 26, Gorman has a minor-league option remaining and can go to Triple-A again in 2027, but the signs are not subtle. The Cardinals are reportedly seeking a stopgap third baseman until top prospect Jesús Báez is ready, which would likely not be the case if they had any belief in Gorman. That projected $3.4 million salary is a high price for a reclamation project ticketed for the minors.

Projected salary: $6.9 million (team control through 2028)

Right-handed power is in short supply throughout baseball and Burger, 31 in April, has hit at least 28 home runs in three of the last four years. He is a one-tool player, though. The home runs come with low batting averages, low on-base percentages, higher-than-average strikeout rates, and little to no defensive or baserunning value. Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young said his team lacked "grit and toughness," whatever that means, and indicated he wants more hitters who grind out at-bats. That's not Burger, who can hit the ball a mile but is not known for making life tough on pitchers. The $6.9 million projection could be deemed too pricey for a player with such a limited skill set.

Projected salary: $6.6 million (team control through 2027)

Doval went from the Yankees to the Pirates at the trade deadline, then from the Pirates to the Giants on waivers in September. He's a former All-Star who led the National League in saves in 2023, two things that have boosted his arbitration salaries. Since 2023, Doval has been a middle reliever who was on the outside of the Circle of Trust™ more often than not. The 29-year-old righty still throws very hard. There's nothing wrong with his arm. It's hard to believe he gets hit as hard as he does sometimes. Doval earned $6.1 million in 2026 and a player cannot have a salary cut by more than 20% during his team control years. That would set Doval's minimum 2027 salary at $4.88 million. I wonder if the Giants would offer him a pay cut, say $5.5M or so, and tell him it's either that or a non-tender. That happens a few times a year around the league.

Projected salary: $6.5 million (team control through 2027)

A fan favorite in San Diego -- "Ho-ly Sheets!" chants are commonplace during his at-bats at Petco Park -- Sheets has fallen by the wayside a bit with the Padres, so much so that he started just one of their six postseason games this year. The 30-year-old is a platoon player who is good against righties more than great and is a defensive liability at both first base and left field. Realistically, Sheets is a platoon DH, and teams rarely pay well for that role unless they're confident they will get big offensive numbers. In the grand scheme of things, the projected $6.5 million isn't much. It is top-of-the-market dollars for this skill set, however.

Projected salary: $1.4 million (team control through 2029)

Two years ago, Blanco threw a no-hitter in his eighth career start. This year, he was so far out of the picture that he pitched once in Houston's last 12 games (two innings at the end of a 13-2 blowout), and the Astros opted to start Peter Lambert on two days' rest with a postseason spot on the line in Game 162. Blanco, who is older than you may realize (he turned 33 in August), returned from Tommy John surgery this summer and had a rough go of it. The pitching-needy Astros could send him to Triple-A next season, as he has a minor-league option remaining, but his stuff was diminished after surgery, and again, they didn't trust him late in the year. You would be surprised at how many cheap pitchers get non-tendered every year. Blanco could join them this week.

#2626. NBA Rookie Rankings: Yaxel Lendeborg debuts at No. 1, Darryn Peterson making up ground in tight race

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This season's NBA Rookie of the Year race has the potential to be one of the closest in league history. While there is no 65-game requirement to win the award — unlike MVP, Defensive Player of the Year and All-NBA honors — playing as many games as possible will be paramount this season in order to claim Rookie of the Year.

That's why Chicago Bulls forward Caleb Wilson faces an uphill climb to win the honor after fracturing his right hand earlier this month. Wilson is set to miss the next 3-5 weeks and will likely lose serious ground to others in his class. He currently has the sixth-best odds (+4000) on FanDuel Sportsbook to win Rookie of the Year.

During the first month of the season, three players have separated themselves at the top: Yaxel Lendeborg, Cameron Boozer, and Darius Acuff Jr. While it's not a guarantee one of those players wins it, if the season ended today, those would be the top vote-getters.

Darryn Peterson and AJ Dybantsa — the first two picks of the 2026 NBA Draft — have some ground to make up during the next four months to get back in the mix.

With the regular season almost a quarter of the way complete, let's dive into our first Rookie of the Year rankings. All odds via FanDuel.

With Steph Curry out, Lendeborg has continued to step up. The oldest player drafted in the first round is coming off a lackluster showing against the Spurs in the NBA Cup, but before that he had three straight games of 23+ points. He is shooting 48.6% from the field and 41.4% from 3. Lendeborg didn't start shooting 3s on a consistent basis until he got to Michigan last season, so knocking down that percentage on 5.4 attempts per night is a positive sign. Fourteen games into the season, Lendeborg is the favorite.

Boozer's raw stats aren't as good as Lendeborg's or even Acuff's, but his impact goes well beyond the box score. His feel for the game is elite for a 19-year-old. Boozer keeps getting better and better as a processor as he continues to log more minutes. The Grizzlies have been one of the league's surprising teams this season. Boozer deserves a ton of credit for that. He wins everywhere he goes, whether at the high school, college, or professional level.

Acuff just turned 20 last week. In 13 games as a teenager, he averaged 25.5 points per game and became the first teenager in NBA history to score at least 275 points and dish out 80 assists in his first 11 games. Acuff is a special offensive talent who is being asked to do more than any rookie in his class. Sacramento is a very bad basketball team, but Acuff makes the Kings somewhat fun to watch. That's a huge credit to him.

The Jazz have been decimated by injuries this season and are currently riding a 12-game losing streak. The one bright side amidst some very bad basketball is how good Peterson has been during that stretch. Peterson had a five-game stretch in which he scored 20 points in each game and shot the ball well from 3. Peterson is the future of Utah's franchise, so getting him as many reps as possible on and off the ball should be the priority.

Dybantsa, the No. 1 overall pick, is averaging 14 shot attempts per game during his first 10 appearances as a pro. He should be taking even more shots. The way the Wizards are using him is confusing at times. Dybantsa is in somewhat of a weird situation because of the Wizards' roster. Washington handed Trae Young a huge contract this offseason that is already aging poorly. Dybantsa should be the focus of the offense. He should be touching the ball and shooting it even more than he is already. I have been impressed with Dybantsa's defense this season.

#2625. As Liam Coen explains Jaguars' late field-goal decision, Giants take offense: 'Disrespectful as hell'

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Down eight points with 3:43 to play, the Jacksonville Jaguars faced fourth-and-goal from the 8-yard line.

Should he bank on his offense, which converted just once on six red-zone trips Sunday, to reverse course amid unfavorable down-and-distance? Or should the Jaguars kick the 26-yard field goal, narrow their deficit to five points and trust the defense that held the New York Giants to three points in the second half to get a stop?

"Fourth-and-8 … what are those percentages of success? I think they're probably less than 5 [percent] in a lot of ways in this league … " Coen said after the game. "Just executing that down-and-distance on a fourth down is kind of challenging, especially when they are zero-blitzing every play. The ball's going to come out. It's like a 'hope' play."

So the Jaguars kicked the field goal and the Giants ran out the clock with two first downs. The Giants won 23-18 after leading for the final 47 minutes.

The Jaguars' strategy of relying on their defense during a day their offense struggled to maintain rhythm did not work out for the visiting team. But the strategy worked well to motivate a Giants team that had lost its own rhythm after halftime.

If the Jaguars thought the Giants weren't going to realize the message their field goal sent, they were mistaken. New York quarterback J.J. McCarthy said "as an offense, we took that personal" as Jacksonville hedged on yet another New York implosion.

"100%, it's disrespectful as hell," right tackle Jermaine Eleumenor said from the postgame locker room. "You're kicking a field goal, you think you're going to get a stop on defense, and if I'm being honest, we were whooping them. On the line of scrimmage, they weren't winning. We won the line of scrimmage, both sides of the ball."

On a day in which the Jaguars were down starting center Robert Hainsey (knee) and lost starting left tackle Walker Little (knee) early in the fourth quarter, a pressure-happy Giants defense kept Trevor Lawrence from ever finding a rhythm.

Arvell Reese brings the heat on Trevor Lawrence in the Giants' victory Sunday.

And on a day in which the Jaguars were onboarding their trade-deadline acquisition starting defenders in defensive tackle Jordan Davis and safety Jessie Bates III, the Giants capitalized on a group adjusting to complex schemes, including with quarterback keepers that powered each of their touchdown drives.

So consider the Giants aware that they were 6-point betting underdogs at home and aware that plenty questioned their division-leading record on account of the below-.500 teams they had beaten.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh called his team's sixth victory "the first real football win."

Edge rusher Abdul Carter said "everybody pretty much counted us out."

"But we took that as disrespect, and we came out with a chip on our shoulder … " said Carter, who finished the game with 2 sacks, 5 quarterback hits and 8 pressures, per Pro Football Focus. "I think we proved that we are worthy. They keep saying we can't beat these teams, we can't beat them. I don't know why they're saying that.

At the end of the first quarter, the Jaguars had not scored a touchdown.

At the end of the second and then third, they hadn't either.

This was a Jacksonville team that entered the week averaging 29.9 points per game, fourth in the league. Its 358.9 yards per game ranked ninth in total offense. So what explained the 20-6 deficit that trickled into the fourth quarter?

"I played really, really poorly today, and you're not going to win many games if I don't play better than that … " said Lawrence, who more than doubled his first three quarters' output with a 164-yard fourth quarter that brought his day to 301 yards, 1 touchdown and 2 interceptions on 25-of-47 (53.2%) passing. "As an offense as a whole, I thought we didn't come out with the aggressiveness and attacking that we normally have.

"I felt like they punched us in the mouth a little bit."

Coen blamed himself for some of his early play-calling, saying he overcompensated for run calls he regretted a week prior by calling three straight passes to set up the opening drive's field goal. The Jaguars strayed on multiple drives from their run, which typically sets up their play-action passing and sets the tone for their physical offensive style. On third-and-medium-to-longs, the Giants pressured Lawrence to the tune of turnovers, incompletions and sacks.

Facing third-and-6 with 7:45 to play in the first quarter, Lawrence thought he could hit receiver Parker Washington out of reach of cornerback Deonte Banks before realizing it was "just a really bad read, really bad decision."

With 11:08 to play in the fourth quarter, Lawrence aimed to throw high and early to avoid an approaching defensive lineman, instead throwing to a spot receiver Jakobi Meyers had yet to reach.

The Giants turned the interceptions into six total points on a day they won by five.

Yet when Jacksonville safety Antonio Johnson stripped running back Cam Skattebo and returned the fumble 42 yards, the Jaguars' offense responded with a turnover on downs. Complementary football eluded the team.

By the time Lawrence found a rhythm in the fourth quarter, hitting receiver Brian Thomas Jr. for an 18-yard touchdown on third-and-10 sandwiched between two field-goal drives, the Jaguars' defense was waning. Perhaps matters would have been different if the officials had ruled differently on Washington's fourth-quarter catch in which he got two feet down but didn't secure the ball without movement as he fell to the ground; but even Lawrence admitted: "It was close, and you can't leave it in the ref's hands."

The Giants celebrated holding onto a lead after letting their last contest slip away to the Washington Commanders in the final minute. Lawrence lamented that his offense's rally was too little, too late.

"It was nice to see the fight at the end of the game and that we were still able to have a shot, thanks to our defense," Lawrence said. "We let our defense down today. They got us a bunch of turnovers and gave us plenty of opportunities to win the game, and we didn't capitalize."

At 6-3-1, the Giants maintained their grip on the NFC East even as the Cowboys improved to 5-6 with a 51-30 win over the Tennessee Titans. Next Gen Stats projects the Giants' chances of making the playoffs at 70% after the win.

The Jaguars, meanwhile, don't just remain atop the AFC South at 7-3. Thanks to their three-game lead in the division, they carry a 98% chance of making the playoffs, per Next Gen Stats.

So postseason contention is not a front-of-mind problem. Cleaning up the errors that the Giants exposed, however, is.

Less than two weeks after trading for Davis and Bates as indications of the belief in the 2026 Jaguars, Jacksonville coaches and executives continue to echo that message.

"They believe in this year and they believe that we can make a push to go to the Super Bowl," cornerback Jourdan Lewis told Yahoo Sports. "Those dreams are still intact, just getting accustomed to the guys and how we want to play and how to attack offenses and how they want to attack our system too. …

Instead, the Jaguars will continue working to acclimate Bates to split-safety looks that differ from his Atlanta responsibilities prior to the trade, and they'll work with Davis as he learns the nuances of coordinator Anthony Campanile's movement calls while remembering that gap integrity, physicality and winning in the trenches will always be the foundation for defensive-line success.

The Jaguars were quiet as they shuffled into the postgame locker room from a rainy MetLife Field. But as they showered and packed up for their flight home, their tone reflected focus more than despair.

There are holes to patch. There is time, in the seven remaining regular-season contests, to patch them.

"It's not the end of the world," Davis told Yahoo Sports of Coen's message. "We have to fix the issues. We have to take our medicine. We have to look ourselves in the mirror and then move forward the next week.

"You don't have time to dwell on your wins and losses in the previous week. You have to move on."

So on the Jaguars will move from their five-point loss and on they'll move from Coen's decision to kick a field goal with 3:43 remaining. That decision will motivate Jacksonville's offensive players to show their head coach next time that they're capable of beating blitzes and performing even when the down and distance doesn't favor them.

And the decision's failure will motivate Jacksonville's defense to shore up the assignments that ceded McCarthy a 19-yard completion up the middle and Skattebo a 5-yard run on second-and-5 to seal the win.

Several Jaguars players echoed their trust in Coen on that decision and beyond. And Lawrence, who said he struggled to read the field efficiently until late in the game, said he understood which part of those late-game analytics moments were in his control.

"It's not my decision at the end of the day," Lawrence said. "It's coach's, but I stand by him. We've got to make plays on first, second and third down so we have a chance to go for it not on fourth-and-7 or 8. It's just a tough down …

"We know who we are. We just didn't play well tonight. If you don't play well, you get beat."

#2622. 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame ballot released: 8 things to know, including newcomers, trends and a prediction

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The ballot for the BBWAA portion of the 2027 Baseball Hall of Fame vote was revealed on Monday, featuring 13 holdovers and 14 newcomers.

The full ballot, in alphabetical order, is Bobby Abreu, Jake Arrieta, Jay Bruce, Mark Buehrle, Asdrúbal Cabrera, Starlin Castro, Wade Davis, Brett Gardner, Cole Hamels, Félix Hernández, Torii Hunter, Jon Lester, Andrew Miller, Dustin Pedroia, Andy Pettitte, Buster Posey, Alex Rodriguez, Francisco Rodríguez, Jimmy Rollins, Pablo Sandoval, Ervin Santana, Kyle Seager, Joakim Soria, Chase Utley, Omar Vizquel, David Wright and Ryan Zimmerman. Newcomers to the ballot are in bold.

As a reminder, players must receive votes on at least 75% of the ballots cast to be inducted into the Hall of Fame with the 2027 class. Those who get at least 5% of the vote can remain on the ballot the following year, and so on, for a maximum of 10 voting cycles. Players who are on the ballot for 10 years without getting 75% of the vote, in addition to players not getting 5% of the vote, fall off the ballot in ensuing years, though that doesn't mean the doors to the Hall are permanently shut.

The results will be announced on Jan. 19, with the induction set for Cooperstown over the summer.

Here's everything else you need to know about the Baseball Hall of Fame this offseason.

As alluded to earlier, there are two different votes each offseason. The BBWAA vote is for former players who have been retired from Major League Baseball for at least five years. It's the most common method in mainstream Hall of Fame ballot discussions. When you hear stuff like "first-ballot Hall of Famer," it means via the BBWAA vote.

Players who don't make it via the BBWAA vote can get extra chances via committees. That's how, for example, Jeff Kent made it last year. Formerly called the Veterans Committee, the Hall of Fame now uses Era Committees, which are divided into two categories: contemporary baseball (1980 to present) and classic (prior to 1980). The contemporary ballot is then split into two, one for players and one for non-players like umpires, executives, pioneers and managers.

Sure enough, this time around, it is a non-player Contemporary Baseball Committee, which looks at "managers, umpires and executives whose most significant career impact was realized since 1980."

We'll dive further into this group as we get closer to the Dec. 6 vote.

Giants legend Buster Posey joins the ballot, and he's one of those cases where I don't think a bunch of people need to delve deeply into his numbers. More than statistics, sometimes we get "feel" guys, as in, you just know he's a Hall of Famer. Posey qualifies there, I would think, for 75% of the electorate. We'll obviously do a deeper dive in the coming weeks, but even without the longevity component (Posey only played in parts of 12 MLB seasons), I think he's in.

As for the rest of the first-timers, the best case would be Jon Lester. Given the way a lot of similar starting pitchers have been treated in voting in recent years, my hunch is he'll be able to hang around on the ballot, but he has a major uphill battle in order to get in.

Then you're looking at Brett Gardner, Ryan Zimmerman, Kyle Seager, the short peak of Jake Arrieta and relief work of Andrew Miller. Good players worth mentioning, of course, but they won't sniff the Hall and it seems likely all behind Posey and Lester are one-and-dones on this ballot, as they'll fall short of 5% of the vote.

This is the sixth year for Alex Rodriguez on the ballot, which means it's the sixth time that I point out that we don't really need much time to go over his case. His numbers say he's one of the 10 best position players of all time, but his ties to PEDs are keeping him out to this point.

He did rise from 37.1% of the vote in 2025 to 40% last time, a new high-water mark. The progress is too modest to believe it's trending toward him getting in, but the number this year is certainly worth watching. If he somehow makes a leap to the 50% range, a deeper conversation might be in order.

While some voters don't mind sending in blank ballots to prove some sort of nebulous point, most impose limits on themselves. Whether it's the actual rule of 10 or some voters saying they'll only vote, for example, for a maximum of three players on any given ballot, relatively weak ballots can leave openings for the best players to show huge gains. With Carlos Beltràn and Andruw Jones getting in last year and only one strong first-year candidate, perhaps Chase Utley can benefit.

Utley is only in his fourth year on the ballot, but he's already made significant gains:

He only needs to add 15.9 points after jumping nearly 20 last voting cycle. The situation is ripe for Utley to either get all the way in or get close enough to where he probably makes the Hall of Fame in 2028.

Some of us are pushing to lower the Hall of Fame standard on modern starting pitchers, given the decreases in workload and how it affects their career numbers. We might be making some headway, but it's still tough sledding. Here are the holdover starting pitchers and their standing:

The bar for relievers to make the Hall of Fame is justly pretty high. We recently saw Billy Wagner make a late move and make it in his last try on the BBWAA ballot. Francisco Rodríguez has had four chances on the ballot and gotten between 7.8% and 11.8% of the vote thus far.

K-Rod ranks sixth all time in saves and has good rate stats. He's worth tracking as it relates to three active relievers. Kenley Jansen is third in saves with a similar number of innings pitched to K-Rod. Craig Kimbrel is fifth and has more than 100 fewer innings pitched. Aroldis Chapman is ninth and in the ballpark of Kimbrel in workload to this point.

If K-Rod continues to have trouble making headway toward induction, does that mean Kimbrel and Chapman will have trouble as well? What about Jansen?

Who else is back on the ballot? A quick look:

Posey is a lock. If the committee era chooses Bochy, Baker and/or Sabean, that would be some nice San Francisco flavor, too, right? I'll predict that committee ballot at a later date, though.

I'll also say Utley's good roll here continues with a relatively weak ballot (at least when you factor in what the PED stain has done to some guys).

On the player side, my 2027 Hall of Fame class prediction is Buster Posey and Chase Utley.

#2619. Sean Payton pays tribute to late Tom Jackson with heartwarming gesture after Broncos win

Broncos head coach Sean Payton made a heartwarming gesture toward the family of the late Denver great Tom Jackson following the Broncos' 38-24 win over the Raiders on Sunday.

Payton told reporters after the game that he had presented Jackson's family with the game ball.

Jackson died on Friday with his death being reported publicly on Sunday by ESPN's Adam Schefter.

"I would be remiss if we didn't start with just honoring Tom Jackson tonight," Payton said. "As a coach, you're always teaching and a lot of these players certainly won't remember him as a player, maybe not as an ESPN media member. But [his family] got a game ball tonight. He's part of the rich history. Tough loss for everyone."

Jackson's family notified ESPN of his passing on Friday and no cause of death was revealed.

Jackson, a fourth-round pick by the Broncos back in 1973, played 14 seasons in Denver and appeared in 191 regular-season games and 10 playoff contests.

He then went on to have an impressive 29-year run at ESPN as a staple alongside Chris Berman.

"I knew him more as an ESPN member with Chris Berman, like everyone grew up with that," Payton said. "I felt like I got to know him. Before even coming here [to Denver], and that was in his ESPN role. But when you get here and you learn more about the history of who was coordinating the defense, what position guys were playing, that kind of thing, it's interesting."

The Broncos released a statement earlier on Sunday, mourning the loss of Jackson when the news was announced.

Denver Broncos linebacker Tom Jackson looks on during a game against the Buffalo Bills at Rich Stadium in Orchard Park, N.Y., Oct. 21, 1984. Getty Images

"The Denver Broncos are heartbroken by the passing of Ring of Fame linebacker Tom Jackson, a cornerstone of the legendary Orange Crush defense and one of the most beloved players in franchise history," the organization said in the statement. "An inspirational leader and fierce competitor, TJ was a proud member of the Broncos' first Super Bowl team that helped establish a winning tradition in Denver. Off the field, Tom carried himself with class, warmth and humility, forging deep connections and lifelong friendships with teammates and throughout Broncos country.

"TJ's dynamic personality, quick wit and football knowledge made him a natural for television and paved the way for a Hall of Fame broadcasting career. For generations of fans, Tom was an iconic fixture on ESPN's Sunday NFL Countdown and NFL Primetime, sharing his thoughtful insight with an unmistakable sense of humor that defined an era of sports broadcasting.

"Above all, TJ loved the Broncos and was a cherished member of our family for more than 50 years. We extend our deepest sympathies to Tom's wife, Jennifer, his daughters, Taylor and Morgan, and all of his family, friends and teammates."

#2617. LeBron James denies report that he asked 76ers for 'patience' with scoring numbers at career low

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Philadelphia 76ers are off to a fantastic start to the 2026-27 season at 12-3, good for first in the Eastern Conference, and perhaps most encouraging for the Sixers is that they're winning without looking like a team playing at its absolute peak.

After a huge offseason adding LeBron James and Jaylen Brown, the Sixers still look like a team figuring out how best to work together, but when it comes time in the fourth quarter to find a way to win, they manage to get the job done. Tyrese Maxey is leading the way with Brown quickly finding his rhythm, but James and Joel Embiid in particular still seem to be feeling it out early in the season.

James, who has never averaged less than 20.9 points per game in his previous 23 seasons, is averaging just 15.1 points per game and his 44.3/22.5/71.7 shooting splits are all career lows or close to it. As James figures things out, ESPN reported that a Sixers source claimed James "asked coaches to be patient with him as he expects to find his rhythm and get his conditioning in line by December as he ramps up."

That report hit social media and caught James' attention, with the 41-year-old star denying ever saying that.

ESPN didn't report a direct quote from James, and it's very possible the Sixers source offered an anecdote that paraphrased James and used the word patience when James never did. That then ended up on a social media graphic and prompted James to shoot it down.

What's fascinating here is it's not a scathing report or even anything particularly juicy. James is struggling with his shot early in the year and seems to be figuring out exactly where he fits in the offense alongside Maxey, Brown and Embiid as a scorer. He's still doing plenty of things well -- including leading the team with 6.9 assists per game and just took over third all-time in assists in NBA history -- and the Sixers are still winning even with James ice cold with his jumper, which history suggests will turn around at some point.

Patience would be prudent from the Sixers with James, whether he wants to use that word or not, and it seems like a matter of when, not if, he gets shots to start falling and the Philly offense becomes even more dynamic.

#2616. MLB rumors: Orioles narrow down search in hunt for starting pitchers; reliever market heating up

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hello and welcome to the last full work week before Thanksgiving. In Major League Baseball, that usually means a slow news week. Those of us wanting a flurry of moves before the CBA expires on Dec. 1 are starting to lose a little hope, but hey, it's still possible. We can start with a fresh batch of rumors and wait for something to come to fruition.

As for the news and rumors for Monday, Nov. 16, let's go.

The Orioles are "operating with the intent of adding" a left-handed starting pitcher, according to the Baltimore Banner. They have extended a qualifying offer to Trevor Rogers and though he's expected to decline it, a reunion remains possible. If not, the Orioles are also reportedly interested in lefty free agents Kris Bubic, Matthew Boyd and David Peterson.

Rogers is the best option here. He finished last season with a 2.90 ERA in his last 20 starts. CBS Sports ranked him as the No. 3 free agent this offseason and the best non-Tarik Skubal pitcher on the market. Here's part of the write-up:

Rogers was never able to fully work off the early season stinkers that inflated his ERA, though this is free agency, and ERA is close to the last thing on the minds of interested teams. You're looking forward in free agency, not backward. The underlying performance indicators are very strong, specifically the ability to get chase and avoid the barrel with four pitches (four-seamer, sinker, changeup, sweeper) that light up analytical models. Rogers also has a fifth-pitch cutter and has shown the ability to hammer the strike zone the last two years.

As things stand, the Orioles' rotation starts with right-handers Kyle Bradish and Shane Baz. Cade Povich is a left-handed option, but they'd clearly like someone else who could qualify as a frontline starter from the left-handed side.

Former Cy Young winner Sandy Alcantara has been involved in trade rumors for years and the Marlins never end up moving him. More of the same this offseason? Probably.

"I expect Sandy to be on the Marlins next year," general manager Peter Bendix told MLB Network.

Alcantara, 31, was 13-11 with a 3.87 ERA, 1.23 WHIP and 153 strikeouts in an MLB-best 214 innings last season. He also grabbed three saves down the stretch as the Marlins started experimenting with using starters in relief on their bullpen day between starts. The 2022 Cy Young winner missed all of 2024 after having Tommy John surgery and started to show flashes of his old self last season. He's now making $21 million in 2027 before hitting free agency.

If the Marlins contend, he'll surely stay put, but if they fall out of contention, it'll be another round of trade rumors.

Free agent left-hander A.J. Minter is getting a lot of interest, per MLB Network. Coming off a season in which he was productive for both the Mets and Twins (in all, a 2.56 ERA, 1.05 WHIP and 41 strikeouts in 45 ⅔ innings), he's being chased by at least the Blue Jays, Nationals, Phillies, Rangers and Royals.

Though he's closed on occasion, Minter has been a quality setup man for most of his 10 MLB years, especially with the Braves in the 2020-24 range. He has good playoff numbers, too, with a 2.88 ERA in 20 career postseason appearances.

The Brewers have acquired right-handed reliever Ryan Walker from the Giants for two minor-league pitchers, the team announced late Sunday. Walker, 30, was up and down in his four years with the Giants, which included time as a closer. He had a 1.91 ERA, 10 saves and 2.8 WAR in 2024, but lost the job of closer during a sub-par 2025 season. Last year, he pitched to a 7.16 ERA and 1.81 WHIP in 32 ⅔ innings.

We have plenty of examples of the Brewers buying low on a player and ending up getting the best version of him, so Walker is the latest to keep an eye on here.

#2615. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.

#2614. Malik Nabers finally has breakout Giants performance after tumultuous stretch

Malik Nabers got the chance to show off his good side.

Coming off two of his quietest and most-criticized performances of the season, the Giants' No. 1 receiver finished with a team-high seven receptions for 55 yards and a touchdown in the team's 23-18 upset of the Jaguars on Sunday at MetLife Stadium.

Nabers' numbers were limited by multiple poor throws from J.J. McCarthy, but the star receiver — who has been targeted for his bad body language and helmet-slamming outbursts — displayed pure joy when he was laughing on the bench with the quarterback after the pair connected for their first touchdown since McCarthy became the starter Oct. 25.

"I just feel like the narrative on me is always all the bad body language things that people have been saying," Nabers said earlier this month. "If it's a problem with anybody, the cameras can stay off me."

After making nine receptions for 111 yards in McCarthy's first start with the Giants in Houston — marking Nabers' fourth straight game with at least 100 yards receiving — the 23-year-old receiver saw repeated double coverages while being held to a total of 87 receiving yards in his next two games, which included a dropped touchdown against the Eagles, and his first career lost fumble in a loss to the Commanders.

Nabers spent much of Sunday being shadowed by former No. 2 overall pick Travis Hunter, but the Giants gave their top offensive option a chance to break free with just over six minutes left in the second quarter.

After moving to the slot — and away from Hunter — Nabers took advantage of a mismatch against Antonio Johnson, blowing past the Jaguars safety for a wide-open 8-yard touchdown catch to give the Giants a 17-6 lead.

New York Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers (1) celebrates a touchdown reception during the first half against the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. Charles Wenzelberg/NY Post

"[Our] coaches just schemed it up, doing a great job to get plays where I'm schemed open," Nabers said. [I've been] seeing a lot of different coverages. [We] watched film and it played out just like we practiced it."

Despite getting off to a slow start in his return from a torn ACL — recording 96 receiving yards in the first three games of the season — and playing with three starting quarterbacks through 10 games, the third-year receiver leads the Giants with 65 catches for 747 yards.

Nabers' 192 receptions through the first 29 games of his career rank third in NFL history, trailing Odell Beckham Jr. (199) and Puka Nacua (194).

"J.J. is gonna give me opportunities to make plays," said Nabers, who received 12 targets. "As much as me and him talk about different plays that we see on film or in practice, he wants to give me the ball."
